# DC Platform — full documentation

> Internal Spring Boot chassis ("platform"): capability starters, references, and decisions. Add one BOM + the starters you need; everything is auto-configured with kill switches under dc.platform.*.


---

<!-- source: index.md -->

# DC Platform

> **Version:** `0.2.0-SNAPSHOT` (release train) · **Spring Boot:** 4.x · **Java:** 25

An internal Spring Boot **chassis**. It gives every service the same cross-cutting behaviour —
correlation IDs, JSON logs, RFC-9457 errors, metrics/tracing, RabbitMQ messaging with a
transactional outbox, and persistence conventions — with **zero configuration**. REST API security
(basic auth) with OpenAPI, and the REST client, follow in the next release
([Spring-native plan](spring-native/plan.md)). You write business logic; the platform does the plumbing.

## Why it exists

Hundreds of services should not each re-decide how to log, how to shape errors, how to propagate a
correlation id, or how to lock a scheduled job. The platform makes those decisions **once**, by
experts, and ships them as defaults you can override. Consistency across services is itself a feature:
operability, security posture, and staffing mobility all improve. See
[why convention over configuration](decisions/adr-010.md).

## 3-minute tour

1. **Generate a service** from the archetype — a running, wired service in under 10 minutes. See the
   [quickstart](quickstart.md).
2. **Add capabilities à la carte.** Each is one starter; a capability you don't add costs you nothing.
   Browse the [capability guides](modules/core.md) and the [platform BOM](reference/bom.md).
3. **Deviate when you must.** Every default is overridable under `dc.platform.<capability>`; every
   capability has a kill switch. The full list is the
   [configuration properties reference](reference/properties.md).
4. **Extend without forking.** Implement an SPI, contribute a bean, and the platform default backs
   off — see the [extension model](concepts/extension-model.md).

## Start here

- **New to the platform?** → [Quickstart](quickstart.md)
- **Why is it shaped this way?** → [Architecture](concepts/architecture.md) ·
  [Dependency constitution](concepts/constitution.md) · [Conventions](concepts/conventions.md)
- **Building a service?** → [Capability guides](modules/core.md) · [Configuration properties](reference/properties.md) ·
  [Error codes](reference/error-codes.md)
- **Operating or upgrading?** → [Runbooks](runbooks/local-dev.md) · [Upgrade notes](upgrade/0.2.0.md) ·
  [Compatibility](reference/compatibility.md)
- **Extending the platform?** → [Extension model](concepts/extension-model.md) · [Testing](testing.md) ·
  [Decision records](decisions/adr-001.md)

## Guarantees

The platform builds and tests on a laptop with **no Docker, no network beyond Maven Central, and no
credentials**. Docker-backed tests are opt-in (`-Pdocker`). The dependency constitution, ArchUnit
rules, coverage, and binary-compatibility checks are all enforced by a green `mvn -T1C verify`.


---

<!-- source: quickstart.md -->

# Quickstart — a new platform service in under 10 minutes

The DC Platform ships a Maven archetype that generates a ready-to-run service wired with the
golden-path chassis (W3C trace correlation, JSON logging, RFC-9457 errors, Bean Validation and
metrics/tracing). You add business logic; the platform does the cross-cutting work.

> **Not secured yet.** Web security (basic auth behind the API gateway) and OpenAPI documentation come with
> the REST API capability in the next release. Until then, keep generated services inside the cluster.

## 1. Generate the service

Prerequisites: JDK 25, Maven 3.9+, and the platform artifacts (archetype, `platform-service-parent`,
BOM, starters) in a repository your Maven can reach — the organization's artifact repository, or your
local repository after `mvn install -DskipTests` in the platform checkout. Run it from any directory
outside a Maven project. A logging + data service:

```bash
mvn org.apache.maven.plugins:maven-archetype-plugin:3.1.2:generate -B \
  -DarchetypeGroupId=ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform \
  -DarchetypeArtifactId=platform-service-archetype \
  -DarchetypeVersion=<platform-version> \
  -DgroupId=com.acme.orders -DartifactId=orders-service -Dpackage=com.acme.orders \
  -Dfeatures=data
```

- **`features`** (optional, default `none`): `none`, or a comma-separated subset of `messaging` and
  `data` — no spaces, no duplicates, any order. Each adds the matching starter and a sample with its
  tests: `messaging/OrderEvents`, `data/Note` + `NoteRepository` + the Flyway migration
  `db/migration/V1__create_note.sql`. Anything else (`kafka`, `restclient`, `data, messaging`,
  `none,data`) fails generation with `unsupported features value …`.
  Structured JSON logging is always on — it is not a feature toggle.
- **`platformVersion`** (optional): the platform release to build against (parent + BOM version).
  Defaults to the archetype's own version, which is the right choice unless you deliberately target
  another train.

> `maven-archetype-plugin` 3.1.2 is the documented, gate-tested version; 3.4.0 also works. On Windows
> PowerShell, quote every `-D` argument (`"-DgroupId=com.acme.orders"`): PowerShell splits unquoted
> arguments at the first `.`, which Maven then reports as "The goal you specified requires a project".

## 2. What you get

```
orders-service/
  pom.xml                     parent=platform-service-parent; golden-path starters (+ feature starters)
  CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md       how coding agents should use platform APIs (read at session start)
  README.md                   run / test / add-a-capability
  src/main/java/.../Application.java
  src/main/java/.../hello/HelloController.java   GET /hello
  src/main/resources/application.yml             offline dev defaults (every profile but prod); local/test/prod
  src/main/java/.../data/, messaging/            feature samples (empty files when the feature is off)
  src/test/java/.../HelloControllerTest.java     @PlatformWebTest
  src/test/java/.../ApplicationSmokeTest.java    @PlatformTest (boots the full context)
  src/test/java/.../StructuredLoggingTest.java   parses the emitted JSON log events: fields, traceId, no tokens
  src/test/java/.../data/NoteRepositoryTest.java Flyway-created schema, CRUD across transactions, rollback, constraint
  src/test/java/.../PlatformConformanceTest.java runs PlatformUsageRules over your code
```

## 3. Build, test, run

```bash
cd orders-service
mvn verify                 # all of the above; no Docker, database, or broker required
mvn spring-boot:run        # boots on :8080 with no profile (JSON logs); -Dspring-boot.run.profiles=local for console logs
java -jar target/orders-service-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar

curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/health/readiness   # open
curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/platform           # capability report (open outside prod)
curl "http://localhost:8080/hello?name=alice"
```

In production run with `--spring.profiles.active=prod` and supply `spring.datasource.*` (data)
externally: `prod` refuses to start without it rather than falling back to an embedded H2 database.

## 4. Add a capability

Nothing is auto-injected (ADR: explicit dependencies). Add the starter, use the platform API:

| Capability | Starter | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Messaging | `platform-starter-messaging-inmemory` / `-rabbit` | `EventPublisher` / `@EventHandler` |
| Transactional outbox | `platform-starter-messaging-outbox` | `OutboxPublisher` in a `@Transactional` method |
| Persistence | `platform-starter-data-jpa` (`-oracle` for Oracle) | Spring Data + platform JPA conventions |

Full catalog: [`docs/modules/`](modules/). Read your service's `CLAUDE.md` before adding cross-cutting
code — the `PlatformConformanceTest` fails the build if you hand-roll what the platform already owns.

## 5. Keep it healthy

The whole path — generate, build, boot, probe — is exercised for every feature combination by
[`tooling/scripts/golden-path.sh`](https://github.com/muhammadallee/dc-platform/blob/main/tooling/scripts/golden-path.sh), the CI `generator-gate` job.
See [`docs/modules/dx.md`](modules/dx.md) for the archetype, `upgrade-check`, and conformance rules.

<!-- source: concepts/architecture.md -->

# Architecture

> **Not yet updated for Spring-native 1.0.0.** Parts of this page still describe capabilities cut in
> Phase 1: JWT security, the validation and events starters, Kafka, cache, locking, storage and others.
> What 1.0.0 ships: [capability status](../spring-native/capability-status.md). The page is rewritten in its capability's phase.

> Condensed from the platform architecture design (§1–2, §14). The full reasoning, candidate
> evaluation, and decision matrix live in the architecture document.

## What the platform is

An internal Spring Boot **chassis**: a set of defaults, not a cage. It gives every service the same
cross-cutting behaviour — correlation IDs, JSON logs, RFC-9457 errors, validation, metrics/tracing,
OpenAPI, security, messaging, persistence conventions — without a framework to learn. You add
business logic; the platform does the plumbing.

## The chosen shape: Hybrid Starter + SPI

Seven architectures were evaluated. Three survived to scoring; the **Hybrid Starter + SPI Platform**
won by a clear margin (weighted 8.48 vs 7.42 for pure starters and 6.58 for feature-modular).

- **Pure Starter-Based** (mirror Spring Boot): best simplicity and learning curve, but no contractual
  extension point — enterprises patch or fork, internals leak, compatibility is hard to promise.
- **Feature Modular** (independently versioned mini-products): maximal autonomy, but a version matrix
  at consumer scale is a support nightmare.
- **Hybrid Starter + SPI** (chosen): feature-sliced capabilities delivered as starters over
  auto-configuration, each multi-provider capability split into `api` / `spi` / `impl` /
  `autoconfigure` / `starter`. One BOM, one release train. Keeps the DX of pure starters, adds a
  contractual extension model, and avoids the version-matrix cost.

Hexagonal architecture was **rejected as the global style but adopted as an internal tactic**: the
platform has no business domain, so forcing every capability through a technology-free core produces
abstraction for its own sake. Where multiple providers genuinely exist (messaging, storage, cache,
locking) the ports-and-adapters idea is exactly right — and survives as the API/SPI/provider split.

## Guiding philosophy

1. **The platform is a set of defaults, not a cage.** Every bean is `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`;
   every feature has a kill switch (`dc.platform.<cap>.enabled=false`); every default is overridable
   in `application.yml`.
2. **Consumers see APIs, extenders see SPIs, nobody sees internals.** Three audiences, three package
   families, three compatibility promises.
3. **Spring Boot mechanisms only.** Auto-configuration, conditions, `ConfigurationProperties`,
   `ObjectProvider`, ordering annotations. No custom lifecycle, registry, or DI.
4. **A capability you don't add costs you nothing.** No transitive reach into Kafka from the logging
   starter. Optional/provided scopes and `@ConditionalOnClass` everywhere.
5. **One train, one BOM, one truth.** All platform modules share a version; consumers import one BOM;
   upgrades are one property change.

## Module taxonomy

A capability `X` is built from up to five module kinds:

| Module | Category | Contains |
|---|---|---|
| `platform-X-api` | API | Consumer-facing interfaces, annotations, value types, exceptions |
| `platform-X-spi` | SPI | Provider/extension contracts (`XProvider`, `XCustomizer`) |
| `platform-X-<provider>` | Implementation | One provider (e.g. `platform-messaging-rabbit`) |
| `platform-X-autoconfigure` | Auto Configuration | `@AutoConfiguration`, `@ConfigurationProperties`, conditions |
| `platform-starter-X[-provider]` | Starter | **No code** — a `pom.xml` aggregating dependencies |

Simple capabilities (one plausible implementation) collapse to `api + autoconfigure + starter`. The
SPI module exists **only** where a second provider is plausible — never speculatively.

## Where this may fail (and the mitigations)

- **Module sprawl** without scaffolding → the archetype and module generator write the boilerplate.
- **API/SPI discipline decay** if gates are relaxed → the gates are merge-blocking; exceptions need
  an ADR.
- **Release-train hostage situations** if one capability is chronically unstable → incubator track.
- **Over-abstraction temptation** → the "SPI only at 2 plausible providers" rule.

## Next

- [Dependency constitution](constitution.md) — the rules and how the build enforces them.
- [Conventions](conventions.md) — properties, packages, error codes, profiles.
- [Extension model](extension-model.md) — customizer tier vs provider tier, and TCK certification.
- [Decision records](../decisions/adr-001.md) — the ten ADRs behind these choices.

<!-- source: concepts/constitution.md -->

# Dependency constitution

> From the architecture design §4. These rules are **executable** (ADR-007): the build fails on any
> violation, so the architecture cannot silently decay.

Capability dependency graph (arrows = "depends on"):

```
starter ──▶ autoconfigure ──▶ impl(provider) ──▶ spi ──▶ api ──▶ core-api
                     └────────── (optional) ──────┘
```

Maximum depth from a starter to JDK-only code is **4 platform hops**.

## Allowed dependencies

1. `api → core-api`, `api → JDK`, `api → spring-core` (only if unavoidable; prefer none).
2. `spi → api` (same capability), `spi → core-api`.
3. `impl → spi, api` (same capability) + its third-party library.
4. `autoconfigure → api, spi` (same capability); `autoconfigure → other capability api` **only**
   with `@ConditionalOnClass` guarding and `<optional>true</optional>`.
5. `autoconfigure → impl` only as `<optional>true</optional>` (compiled against, activated
   conditionally).
6. `starter → autoconfigure + exactly the impl(s) it names + that impl's driver`.
7. `test-support → api, spi` (+ test libs).
8. Everything → `platform-build-tools` (build-time only).

## Forbidden dependencies

1. `api → spi | impl | autoconfigure | starter`. **API must never depend on implementation.**
2. `impl → impl` (cross-provider or cross-capability).
3. `starter → starter`.
4. `spi → impl`.
5. Any platform module → examples or any application.
6. Any module → another capability's `spi`, `impl`, or `internal` packages.
7. `core-api → anything platform` (it is the root).
8. Compile-scope Spring Boot starters inside `api`/`spi` modules.

## Quantitative limits

- Maximum platform dependency depth: **4**.
- Maximum fan-out per module: **api ≤ 1** platform dep, **spi ≤ 2**, **impl ≤ 3**,
  **autoconfigure ≤ 6** (incl. optionals), **starter ≤ 4**.
- Any non-core module with fan-in > 5 must justify or split.
- **Zero cycles.**

## How the build enforces it

The rules are fitness functions, evaluated on every `mvn verify`:

- **maven-enforcer** — `banCircularDependencies` plus the custom `PlatformLayerRule` in
  `platform-build-tools`, which reads each module's category from its coordinates and fails the build
  on any forbidden edge, naming the violated edge and the fix.
- **ArchUnit** — the `PlatformArchRules` rule-jar runs in every module's test phase
  (`ArchConstitutionTest`), catching package-level violations (e.g. importing another capability's
  `.internal`).
- **japicmp** — binary-compatibility gate over `-api`/`-spi` packages (armed after the first tag);
  `.internal` packages are excluded.
- **dependency-convergence** — one version per third-party across the reactor.

A gate that never fails might be a gate that never runs: seed a forbidden `starter → starter` edge on
a scratch branch and confirm the build fails with the right message.

- [Architecture](architecture.md) · [Conventions](conventions.md) · [ADR-007](../decisions/adr-007.md).

<!-- source: concepts/conventions.md -->

# Conventions

> Properties, packages, error codes, and profiles. Conventions are **API** (ADR-010): every
> capability works with zero configuration; configuration exists only to *deviate*, and changing a
> default is a breaking change.

## Properties

- Every platform property lives under `dc.platform.<capability>`.
- `@ConfigurationProperties` classes are **immutable records** with constructor binding; every
  property has a default in code **and** in config metadata (so IDEs autocomplete every key).
- Every capability has a kill switch: `dc.platform.<capability>.enabled` (default `true`,
  `matchIfMissing = true`).
- Renames require a deprecation window with `additional-spring-configuration-metadata.json`
  deprecation entries — property keys are a contract.

The full, generated list is the [configuration properties reference](../reference/properties.md).

## Packages

For a capability `messaging`:

```
ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform.messaging                 → public API (stable)
ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform.messaging.annotation      → public annotations
ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform.messaging.spi             → SPI (stable-for-extenders)
ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform.messaging.config          → @ConfigurationProperties (stable keys)
ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform.messaging.autoconfigure   → @AutoConfiguration (names stable for exclude=)
ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform.messaging.<provider>          → provider public surface (small)
ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform.messaging.<provider>.internal → internals (no guarantees)
ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform.messaging.internal        → internals (no guarantees)
ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform.messaging.migration       → deprecated bridges during a deprecation window
```

`*.internal.*` is excluded from javadoc, excluded from japicmp, and flagged by an ArchUnit rule if
imported from application code.

## Error codes

- Every platform error carries a stable `DC-<CAP>-<NNNN>` code (`DC-CORE-0500`, `DC-MSG-0001`, …).
- Codes are **unique platform-wide**, enforced by the build-time error-code registry gate.
- Codes surface in RFC-9457 problem responses. The generated list is the
  [error-codes reference](../reference/error-codes.md); see also the [errors module](../modules/errors.md).

## Profiles

- `local` — console logs, in-memory/H2 providers; the default for laptops and the untagged test suite.
- Real backing services (RabbitMQ, Oracle Free) come from `docker-compose.local.yml`; see the
  [local development runbook](../runbooks/local-dev.md).
- Docker-backed tests are tagged `@Tag("docker")` and only run under `-Pdocker`.

## Auto-configuration conditions (evaluation order)

`@ConditionalOnClass` (provider on classpath) → `@ConditionalOnProperty` (kill switch,
`matchIfMissing = true`) → `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` (user override). Cheapest-to-evaluate first.

## Next

- [Dependency constitution](constitution.md) · [Extension model](extension-model.md) · [ADR-010](../decisions/adr-010.md).

<!-- source: concepts/extension-model.md -->

# Extension model

> **Not yet updated for Spring-native 1.0.0.** Parts of this page still describe capabilities cut in
> Phase 1: JWT security, the validation and events starters, Kafka, cache, locking, storage and others.
> What 1.0.0 ships: [capability status](../spring-native/capability-status.md). The page is rewritten in its capability's phase.

> From the architecture design §6. One pattern for all extension (ADR-008): **implement the SPI, ship
> your own auto-configuration, register it, order it before the platform's default.** Platform
> defaults are all `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`, so your bean wins. **No platform module is ever
> modified.**

## Two tiers

**Customizer tier — tweak the default.** Contribute `*Customizer` beans (`RestClientCustomizer`,
`ProblemDetailCustomizer`, `RabbitTemplateCustomizer`, …). The platform collects them via
`ObjectProvider<List<…Customizer>>.orderedStream()` and applies them in `@Order`. You add behaviour
without replacing beans.

**Provider tier — replace the engine.** Implement a capability SPI and contribute the bean; the
platform default backs off. Certify your provider against the capability's TCK.

## Provider examples

| Add a new… | Implement | Register | Platform behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|
| Messaging provider (e.g. Pulsar) | `EventTransport` from `messaging-spi` | your autoconfigure + starter | façade binds to any `EventTransport`; default backs off via `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` |
| Tracing provider | Micrometer `Tracer` + `ObservationCustomizer` | bean | Micrometer *is* the SPI; platform never wraps tracing itself |

## TCK certification

Each multi-provider capability ships a `platform-<cap>-tck` test-jar with an abstract JUnit class.
A provider proves conformance by extending it and pointing it at their implementation — the same
contract the platform's own providers pass. See [testing](../testing.md) and the module pages for
[messaging](../modules/messaging.md), storage, locking,
flags, and ratelimit.

## Next

- [Conventions](conventions.md) · [Dependency constitution](constitution.md) · [ADR-008](../decisions/adr-008.md) · [ADR-003](../decisions/adr-003.md).

<!-- source: concepts/discovery.md -->

# Layered discovery

The platform is designed to advertise itself at every moment a developer or agent needs it, so nobody
has to guess. Each layer is generated or enforced from code — there are no hand-maintained mirrors that
can rot. The five layers map to the five times you reach for the platform.

## Layer 0 — code time (signals inside the jars)

What you learn while reading or importing a platform artifact.

- **apiguardian `@API(status, since)`** on every public API/SPI type, so stability (STABLE /
  EXPERIMENTAL / DEPRECATED / INTERNAL) is readable straight from the jar. Enforced by an ArchUnit
  rule; `DEPRECATED` must co-occur with `@Deprecated`. See [conventions](conventions.md).
- **FailureAnalyzers** turn the top misconfigurations into a Boot *Description / Action* block whose
  Action names the exact fix (the starter, property, or doc anchor) — a startup failure teaches.

## Layer 1 — scaffold time (the archetype)

A generated service starts correct: `platform-service-parent`, a conformance test, and the agent /
catalog files `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `.mcp.json`, and `catalog-info.yaml`. See
[developer experience](../modules/dx.md).

## Layer 2 — build time (teaching in the service build)

The service's own build refuses the wrong thing and says why.

- **Dependency bans** in `platform-service-parent`: declaring `spring-rabbit` directly fails the build
  with the starter to use instead.
- **`PlatformUsageRules`** (a conformance test the archetype wires in): no hand-rolled
  `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler`, no `new ObjectMapper()`, no `System.getenv`, no `Thread.sleep` in
  production — each violation names the platform alternative.

## Layer 3 — on demand (agents ask, tools rewrite)

- **MCP server** (`platform-mcp-server --stdio`): six read-only tools answer authoritative questions —
  `find_capability`, `property_lookup`, `error_code_lookup`, `usage_example`, `list_starters`,
  `platform_version` — from a build-time `platform-index.json`.
- **Skill** (`platform-skill.zip`): a Claude Skill generated from the same index, tuned to trigger on
  platform vocabulary.
- **Adopt/upgrade recipes** (`platform-migrations`, OpenRewrite): `AdoptPlatform` swaps banned deps for
  starters and flags hand-rolled advice for review; per-train `UpgradeTo_X_Y` skeletons carry
  deprecation-driven rewrites.
- **`llms.txt` / `llms-full.txt`**: the docs, curated from the nav for LLMs.

## Layer 4 — org time (adoption is visible)

- **`platform.capability.active{capability}`** gauge and the `platform.version` common tag feed the
  [adoption dashboard](../operations/adoption.md): trains in production, capability adoption, and who is
  behind.
- **`catalog-info.yaml`** registers each service (with its `dc.platform/train`) in the org catalog.

## Why generated, not written

Every artifact above is produced at build time from the one source that is already authoritative — the
BOM, the config metadata, the error-code registry, the docs pages, the deprecation metadata. Freshness
tests fail the build if a generated surface drifts from the code, so the discovery layers stay true.


---

<!-- source: modules/core.md -->

# Core

The smallest useful chassis: request correlation by W3C trace ID, context propagation, the platform
exception model, and the startup capability banner.

## What you get

- **Correlation = the W3C trace ID** — the only correlation identifier is the trace ID of the
  current span. A request carrying a valid `traceparent` continues that trace; a missing or invalid
  one starts a new trace (Boot's observation filter and the OpenTelemetry W3C propagator do this — the
  platform never parses the header). The platform filter then opens `RequestContext` with the trace
  ID, so `RequestContext.correlationId()`, the SLF4J `MDC` (`traceId`, `spanId`) and every error body
  (`traceId`) carry it. No custom correlation header is read, generated, echoed or sent: a caller's
  `X-Correlation-Id` is ignored. A `traceparent` the propagator did not continue is logged only as a fixed DEBUG marker
  with the header's length — no header content ever reaches a log line.
- **Works when unsampled** — unsampled spans still carry a valid trace ID, so correlation does not
  depend on `management.tracing.sampling.probability`.
- **Every dispatch** — the context is re-established on ASYNC redispatches (a `Callable`/`CompletableFuture`
  handler that completes or fails later) and on the servlet ERROR dispatch (`sendError`, exceptions
  escaping the filter chain), so those error bodies carry the request's `traceId` too.
- **Context propagation** — the platform turns on Boot's own
  `spring.task.execution.propagate-context`, and registers a Micrometer `ThreadLocalAccessor` for
  `RequestContext`: `@Async` methods and Boot-built executors see the caller's trace in
  `RequestContext` and the MDC, and pool threads are clean after each task. Executors you build
  yourself need `ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator` (or `ContextSnapshot.wrap`) to get the same.
- **Exception model** — subclass `PlatformException` with a stable `ErrorCode`
  (`DC-<CAP>-<NNNN>`); the errors capability maps them to RFC-9457 problem responses.
- **Capability banner** — one INFO line at startup listing every active platform capability:
  `platform: core[ACTIVE], messaging[ACTIVE] (rabbit)`.
- **API markers** — `@PlatformApi` (SemVer-guaranteed) and `@PlatformInternal` (no guarantees).

## Starter coordinates

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform</groupId>
  <artifactId>platform-starter-core</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

The core starter brings the tracer correlation needs: the Micrometer Tracing OpenTelemetry bridge and
Boot's tracing/observation auto-configuration (no exporter — spans are only shipped when the
observability starter adds one). A service with just core + errors + logging therefore still continues
an inbound `traceparent` into its logs and error bodies. If tracing is removed or disabled, requests
run with no correlation context and error bodies omit `traceId` — the platform never invents an id.

## Zero-config behavior

On a servlet web app: the correlation filter runs at order `HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + 10` — after Boot's
`ServerHttpObservationFilter` (`HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + 1`, which continues or starts the trace) and
before Spring Security (`-100`), so 401/403 bodies and security log lines already carry the trace ID.
In any app: Boot's task executors propagate context, and the banner logs once the context is ready.
Non-web apps get no filter; everything else is unchanged.

## Properties

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `dc.platform.core.enabled` | `true` | Kill switch for the whole capability (tier `DEFAULT_ON`). |
| `dc.platform.core.banner-enabled` | `true` | Log the startup capability banner. |
| `spring.task.execution.propagate-context` | `true` (platform default; Boot's is `false`) | Boot's own context propagation for its executors. |

Removed (deprecated, level `error` — setting them has no effect): `dc.platform.core.correlation.header-name`,
`dc.platform.core.correlation.generate-if-missing`. There is no header to name and nothing to generate:
a request without a valid `traceparent` always starts a new trace.

## Customize

- Contribute a capability line to the banner from your own auto-configuration:

```java
@Bean
CapabilityDescriptor myCapabilityDescriptor() {
    return new CapabilityDescriptor("mycap", "ACTIVE", "provider-x");
}
```

- Read the correlation id anywhere on a request (or `@Async`) thread:

```java
RequestContext.correlationId()
        .map(CorrelationId::value)          // the W3C trace ID
        .ifPresent(traceId -> receipt.setSupportReference(traceId));
```

## Replace / Disable

Overrides are by type, under any bean name (D98), the way Boot backs off its own filters:

- Define your own `CorrelationIdFilter` bean (a subclass, say) to replace the filter. The platform
  registration backs off and Boot registers yours; `CorrelationIdFilter` is `Ordered` at
  `CoreContextAutoConfiguration.FILTER_ORDER` and runs on REQUEST, ASYNC and ERROR dispatches, so it
  keeps the platform's position.
- Define a `FilterRegistrationBean<CorrelationIdFilter>` to control the registration yourself (order,
  URL patterns, or `setEnabled(false)`). Keep it after the observation filter, or there is no span yet:

  ```java
  @Bean
  FilterRegistrationBean<CorrelationIdFilter> correlationRegistration(Tracer tracer) {
      var registration = new FilterRegistrationBean<>(new CorrelationIdFilter(tracer));
      registration.setOrder(CoreContextAutoConfiguration.FILTER_ORDER);
      registration.setDispatcherTypes(DispatcherType.REQUEST, DispatcherType.ASYNC, DispatcherType.ERROR);
      return registration;
  }
  ```

  Unrelated filters and registrations never affect the platform's.
- Define a `PlatformBannerRunner` bean (subclass it and override `describe`) to change the banner, or
  set `dc.platform.core.banner-enabled=false` and add your own `ApplicationRunner`. Other
  `ApplicationRunner` beans never suppress the banner.
- Capability descriptors are one bean per capability, so they back off **by name**, like Boot's health
  indicators (D97): a bean named `coreCapabilityDescriptor` replaces the core entry. A descriptor under
  any other name is simply one more entry.
- `dc.platform.core.enabled=false` switches the capability off wholesale (no correlation context, no
  platform executor default); tracing itself keeps working.

## Error codes

None — core defines the model (`PlatformException`, `ErrorCode`); see the errors capability for the
codes the platform maps.

## Testing

`RequestContext.open(id, extras)` is `@PlatformInternal` but usable from tests to establish a
context around code under test (try-with-resources). For a real request, send a `traceparent`
(`00-<32 hex trace id>-<16 hex span id>-01`) and assert the trace ID in the response's ProblemDetail or
the JSON log's `traceId`; the archetype's `HttpIntegrationTestSupport` does exactly that.

## Upgrading from the `X-Correlation-Id` model

Callers that sent `X-Correlation-Id` should send `traceparent` instead (any OpenTelemetry/W3C client
does this automatically). Log queries on `correlationId` become queries on `traceId`; ProblemDetail
consumers read `traceId`. `CorrelationId` and `RequestContext.correlationId()` keep their API.

## Local dev notes

No Docker, no network: everything in this capability is in-process. The banner is the quickest
smoke check that platform auto-configuration ran at all — if it is missing, check that the
starter is on the classpath and `dc.platform.core.enabled` is not `false`.


---

<!-- source: modules/errors.md -->

# Errors

RFC-9457 problem responses with stable, machine-readable error codes: throw a
`BusinessException`, get a correct `application/problem+json` body with `code`, `traceId`,
`timestamp` and `retryable` — correlated with the JSON log line by the W3C trace ID.

## What you get

- **Business exception hierarchy** — `BusinessException` (422 by default), `NotFoundException`
  (404), `ConflictException` (409); each carries an `ErrorCode` (`DC-<CAP>-<NNNN>`) that becomes
  the problem `type`/`title` and the `code` extension.
- **Platform exception mapping** — any other `PlatformException` maps to 500 with its own code;
  a data-access failure maps to 409/503 with a `DC-DATA-*` code (below); anything else unmapped maps
  to 500 with `DC-CORE-0500`.
- **Data-access failures** — recognised anywhere in the cause chain, whether Spring translated them
  (`DataIntegrityViolationException`, `OptimisticLockingFailureException`, …) or not (raw
  Hibernate/JPA/JDBC types from code that uses the `EntityManager` directly; SQLState `23`/`40`/`08`):
  constraint violation → 409 `DC-DATA-0409`, concurrent update or lock → 409 `DC-DATA-0410`,
  unavailable database or timeout → 503 `DC-DATA-0503` (`retryable: true`). The detail is fixed — the
  database's message, which names SQL, tables and constraints, never reaches the caller; it is logged
  at WARN on the request's trace. A SQL bug (bad grammar, unknown table) stays a 500. **No 5xx body ever carries an exception
  message** — every 5xx gets the generic detail `An unexpected error occurred.`; the full exception
  goes to the log with the trace ID. 4xx business exceptions keep their application-authored message.
- **Framework errors get the same contract** — Spring MVC's own rejections (404, 405, 406, 415, …) keep
  their statuses and gain `code` (`DC-CORE-0499`), `traceId`, `timestamp`, `retryable`; an unreadable
  or malformed body is `DC-CORE-0410` with a fixed detail (the JSON parser's message, which names
  classes and offsets, never reaches the caller).
- **`retryable`** — `true` for 429, 502, 503, 504, otherwise `false`: a hint for clients deciding
  whether to retry the identical request after backing off.
- **The servlet error page too** — `PlatformErrorController` replaces Boot's `BasicErrorController`:
  a filter's `sendError(…)` or an exception escaping the filter chain is rendered as
  `application/problem+json` (whatever the `Accept` header) with `instance` = the original URI and
  the request's `traceId`. Define your own `ErrorController` bean to replace it.
- **Security denials pass through** — an `AccessDeniedException`/`AuthenticationException` thrown in
  a controller (e.g. method security) is handed back to Spring Security, which renders the platform
  403/401, instead of being swallowed into a 500.
- **Validation mapping** — `@Valid` body failures and method-validation
  `ConstraintViolationException`s map to 400 with an `errors[]` extension
  (`field`, `message`). `rejectedValue` is **omitted by default** — rejected values are raw user
  input and may be personal data; turn it on with `dc.platform.errors.include-rejected-values=true`,
  and even then password/secret/token-shaped fields are `REDACTED`.
- **Customization SPI-lite** — `ProblemDetailCustomizer` beans applied in `@Order` to every
  outgoing problem body.
- **Error-code registry** — build-time gates assert code format and platform-wide uniqueness:
  one scans the classpath and exports `target/error-codes.csv` (feeds the reference), the other reads
  the production sources of every platform module, so a duplicate anywhere fails the build.

## Starter coordinates

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform</groupId>
  <artifactId>platform-starter-errors</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

The starter brings no web stack — your service already chooses one; outside servlet web apps the
advice backs off entirely.

## Zero-config behavior

On a servlet web app, two `@RestControllerAdvice` beans register: the constraint-violation
advice at `@Order(0)` and the catch-all platform advice at lowest precedence, so your own advice
beans always win for your exceptions. Framework exceptions (404 no-handler, 405, 415, …) keep
their proper statuses — the platform advice extends `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler`.

```java
throw new NotFoundException(new ErrorCode("DC-ORDER-0404"), "order 42 not found");
```

```json
{
  "type": "urn:dc:problem:DC-ORDER-0404",
  "title": "DC-ORDER-0404",
  "status": 404,
  "detail": "order 42 not found",
  "instance": "/orders/42",
  "code": "DC-ORDER-0404",
  "traceId": "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef",
  "timestamp": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z",
  "retryable": false
}
```

## Properties

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `dc.platform.errors.enabled` | `true` | Kill switch for the whole capability. |
| `dc.platform.errors.include-stacktrace` | `false` | Add a `stacktrace` extension (debug only). |
| `dc.platform.errors.type-base-uri` | `urn:dc:problem:` | Base URI forming the problem `type`. |
| `dc.platform.errors.map-validation` | `true` | Map validation failures to 400 + `errors[]`. |
| `dc.platform.errors.include-rejected-values` | `false` | Echo invalid values as `errors[].rejectedValue` (raw user input; credentials stay redacted). |

The default `type` prefix `urn:dc:problem:` is a neutral, non-dereferenceable identifier (RFC 9457
allows a `type` that is not a locator): clients match on it, nothing tries to fetch it, and it points at
no host the platform does not own. Once your organisation publishes error documentation, set
`type-base-uri` to that `https://…/` base so `type` links to the page for each code (D99).

(Hand-written until the generated reference lands in phase 14.)

## Customize

```java
@Bean
@Order(10)
ProblemDetailCustomizer tenantCustomizer() {
    return (detail, source) -> detail.setProperty("tenant", TenantContext.current());
}
```

Customizers run last, in order, on every problem body the platform emits.

## Replace / Disable

- Define a `PlatformExceptionHandler` (subclass) bean, or any bean named `platformExceptionHandler`,
  to replace the main advice; likewise `PlatformConstraintViolationHandler` /
  `platformValidationExceptionHandler` for the constraint-violation advice; any `ErrorController` bean
  replaces the error page; a bean named `errorsCapabilityDescriptor` replaces the banner line.
- `dc.platform.errors.map-validation=false` reverts validation failures to Spring's default
  problem body.
- `dc.platform.errors.enabled=false` switches the capability off wholesale.

## Error codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `DC-CORE-0400` | Request validation failed (`errors[]` lists the violations). |
| `DC-CORE-0410` | Request body unreadable or malformed (e.g. invalid JSON). |
| `DC-CORE-0499` | Any other request the servlet stack rejected (404, 405, 406, 415, …); status preserved. |
| `DC-CORE-0500` | Unhandled exception; generic body, full details in the log. |
| `DC-DATA-0409` | 409 — the request conflicts with stored data (unique, foreign-key, NOT NULL or check constraint). |
| `DC-DATA-0410` | 409 — the data was changed or is locked by another request; reload and retry. |
| `DC-DATA-0503` | 503 — the database is unavailable: no pooled connection in time, statement/transaction timeout, lost connection. Retryable. |
| `DC-SEC-0401` | Missing or unacceptable credentials (security entry point). |
| `DC-SEC-0403` | Authenticated, but lacking the required authority (security denied handler). |

Applications register their own codes by declaring `static final ErrorCode` constants — the
registry gate picks them up automatically.

## Testing

The advices are plain beans:
`MockMvcBuilders.standaloneSetup(controller).setControllerAdvice(handler)` exercises mappings
without a full context. Open a `RequestContext` (try-with-resources) around the call to see the
`traceId` extension. Inject a fixed `Clock` bean to make `timestamp` deterministic.

## Local dev notes

No Docker, no network. Quick smoke check: `curl -s localhost:8080/nonexistent | jq .type` — a
`urn:dc:problem:…` URI proves the advice is active; Spring's default body means the
starter is missing or the kill switch is off.

<!-- source: modules/logging.md -->

# Logging

Structured JSON logs on stdout with service identity and correlation, credentials and common PII
masked, configured before the application context exists — and readable console output when a human
is watching.

## What you get

- **JSON by default** — one logstash-encoded line per event with ECS-ish fields:
  `@timestamp`, `level`, `logger`, `message`, `service`, `traceId`, `spanId` (and every other MDC
  entry), `stack_trace`.
- **Console for humans** — activate the `local` profile and output falls back to Boot's
  human-readable console format (explicit `dc.platform.logging.format` always wins).
- **Correlation built in** — the core filter publishes the W3C `traceId` (and `spanId`) to the MDC; the encoder
  lifts MDC entries into JSON fields, so log lines correlate with problem responses for free. These two
  are the only MDC keys platform code writes.
- **Redaction** — in every string the JSON encoder writes (message, MDC values, structured arguments,
  exception message, stack trace) the platform replaces with `****`:
  - JWTs (three dot-separated base64url segments whose first decodes to a JSON object, whitespace
    around it allowed); whatever follows `Bearer` (so prose such as "Bearer token missing" reads
    "Bearer **** missing"); `Basic` credentials that decode to `user:password`;
  - the value after a credential key (`password`, `passwd`, `pwd`, `secret`, `client_secret`, `token`,
    `access_token`, `refresh_token`, `id_token`, `api-key`/`apikey`, `authorization`, and compound keys
    ending in one of them or in `cookie`: `session_token`, `db-password`, `smtpSecret`, `sessionCookie`)
    in `key=value`,
    `key: value`, `"key":"value"` and `key='value'` text — quoted values whole (escapes included, an
    unterminated quote to the end), quotes kept;
  - everything after `Cookie:` / `Set-Cookie:` up to the end of the line (all pairs, quoted ones too);
  - the whole value — of any type (string, number, boolean, `byte[]`, object, array) — of an MDC entry or
    structured-argument field, at any depth, whose **name** is one of those keys or `cookie` /
    `set-cookie`, or ends in one of them ignoring case, `-` and `_` (`sessionToken`, `x-auth-token`,
    `db_password`); in the formatted `message` such an argument reads `password=****` (`****` for a
    value-only `v(...)`);
  - Emirates ID numbers (`784-YYYY-NNNNNNN-C`, dashes optional) and Luhn-valid card numbers starting
    2–6: 13–19 contiguous digits, or the printed layouts `4111 1111 1111 1111` (optionally `+1..3`
    digits) and `3782 822463 10005`, with one consistent space or dash separator — in text and when
    logged as a number;
  - e-mail addresses;
  - phone numbers: international with a `+` or `00` prefix (`+971 50 123 4567`, `00971501234567`,
    `+44 20 7946 0958`) and UAE mobiles in local form (`050 123 4567`, `0501234567`).

  Timestamps, epoch millis, trace/span IDs (also hex IDs with digit runs inside), UUIDs, IP addresses,
  version strings, `Object@1a2b3c` identity strings and ordinary numeric IDs are left alone. The
  top-level `traceId`/`spanId` fields are never masked while they hold W3C hex IDs; no other field name
  exempts a value (the encoder's own `level`/`logger` included). Masking is linear in the input length
  and stack-safe on long values. Residual risks: a numeric ID that happens to
  be a Luhn-valid 13–19 digit number starting 2–6, or a 10-digit ID starting `050`–`058`, is masked;
  UAE landlines written without a prefix (`04 123 4567`) are **not** masked — add a pattern if you log
  them; a card number your code logs as a top-level field named `traceId`/`spanId` that is also a
  16-character hex string is not masked.
- **No forged lines** — JSON string escaping keeps CR/LF, quotes and embedded JSON inside one field, so
  user input cannot add a line or a field. In JSON mode Boot's startup banner is off
  (`spring.main.banner-mode=off`, overridable), so every stdout line is one JSON object.
- **`Kv.of(key, value)`** — structured argument helper that stays readable in console format.
- **`LogSanitizer` beans** — your own scrubbing, applied in `@Order` before the platform masks run, to
  MDC values and to keyed arguments — `Kv.of`, Logstash `kv(...)`/`v(...)`/`value(...)` and
  `entries(...)` — in both the structured field and the argument's text in `message`, but not to the
  platform's own top-level fields. Supported values: strings, numbers, maps, collections and object
  arrays, nested in any combination; each value is sanitized under its own key (map entries under
  theirs, array elements under the enclosing field's). Other objects (beans) are sanitized field by
  field in the JSON output only; in `message` they keep their `toString()`, over which the platform
  masks still run (`fields(bean)` likewise). A `Kv` or marker nested inside a value is treated like a
  top-level one (a nested `Kv` is written `{"<key>": value}` in JSON, so its credential name masks it);
  chained markers (`append(...).and(...)`) render each one, `, `-joined. `raw(...)` JSON is parsed and
  masked like any other structured value, in the JSON field and in `message` (escapes decoded, member
  order and duplicate names kept, numbers exact; `message` shows it decoded, `{name=value}`, like
  other structured values); raw text that is not exactly one JSON value (invalid, trailing text) is
  written as a JSON string, escapes decoded, under the pattern masks (D109). Card numbers logged as a
  `double` (`4111111111111111.0`, also inside a `double[]`) are masked too; `LogSanitizer` beans run
  before that check. In `message`, a value nested more than 64 levels deep, or a container that
  contains itself, reads `****`. An argument whose rendering throws reads
  `[unrenderable]` in `message`, and the exception text is not reported anywhere (stderr, Logback
  status).

## Starter coordinates

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform</groupId>
  <artifactId>platform-starter-logging</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

## Zero-config behavior

An `EnvironmentPostProcessor` (the platform's one `spring.factories` registration — logging must
configure before the context) defaults `logging.config` to the shipped `logback-platform.xml`
through a lowest-precedence property source named `platform-logging-defaults` (visible in
`/actuator/env`). `service` defaults to `spring.application.name`, then `application`.

```json
{"@timestamp":"2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z","message":"login for alice with password=****",
 "logger":"ae.gov.dc.orders.OrderService","level":"INFO","service":"orders",
 "traceId":"0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef","spanId":"b7ad6b7169203331"}
```

## Properties

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `dc.platform.logging.enabled` | `true` | Kill switch for the whole capability. |
| `dc.platform.logging.format` | `json` | `json` or `console`; unset + `local` profile ⇒ console. |
| `dc.platform.logging.include-mdc` | `true` | Copy MDC entries into JSON fields. |
| `dc.platform.logging.service-name` | `${spring.application.name}` | Service stamped on every line. |
| `dc.platform.logging.mdc.include` | empty | Strict mode: when set, only `traceId`, `spanId` and these MDC keys are written. |
| `dc.platform.logging.redaction.enabled` | `true` | Mask credentials and PII in JSON output. |
| `dc.platform.logging.redaction.patterns` | empty | Extra regular expressions whose matches are masked. |

(Hand-written until the generated reference lands in phase 14.)

## Customize

- `dc.platform.logging.service-name=customs-orders` overrides the stamped service identity.
- `dc.platform.logging.mdc.include=tenant,channel` keeps only those MDC keys (plus `traceId`/`spanId`)
  — use it when other libraries put noisy or sensitive entries in the MDC.
- `dc.platform.logging.redaction.patterns[0]=CASE-\d{6}` masks your own identifiers too.
- A `LogSanitizer` bean scrubs by key:

  ```java
  @Bean
  LogSanitizer customerNameSanitizer() {
      return (key, value) -> "customerName".equals(key) ? "C***" : value;
  }
  ```
- `dc.platform.logging.include-mdc=false` drops MDC fields (correlation included — rarely wise).

## Replace / Disable

- Set `logging.config` to your own file — any user-set value outranks the platform default. Your file
  then decides about masking: reuse
  `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform.logging.autoconfigure.PlatformJsonEncoder` or accept that
  nothing is masked.
- `dc.platform.logging.format=console` keeps Boot's default logging everywhere (no masking).
- `dc.platform.logging.redaction.enabled=false` writes values unmasked (also removes the
  `LogSanitizerRegistry` bean that hands your `LogSanitizer` beans to the encoder).
- `dc.platform.logging.enabled=false` switches the capability off wholesale.

## Error codes

None — logging fails soft by design; a broken logging setup must never take the service down. A
`LogSanitizer` that throws is skipped for that value; the platform masks still apply.

## Testing

`OutputCaptureExtension` + a real `SpringApplicationBuilder(...).run()` exercises the whole
chain (EPP → logback → encoder); assert JSON keys on `output.getOut()`. Logback state is
JVM-global — `((LoggerContext) LoggerFactory.getILoggerFactory()).reset()` after such tests.
`LogSanitizer` beans are handed to the encoder once the context has started; with several contexts in
one JVM the most recently started one wins.

## Local dev notes

Run with `--spring.profiles.active=local` for readable console lines. Console output is for humans and
is **not** masked, and a CR/LF in a message can split a console line — never ship console format to log
aggregation. If production output is not JSON: check the banner line `logging[ACTIVE] (json|console)` —
it reports the effective format decision, and `/actuator/env` shows whether `platform-logging-defaults`
was outranked.


---

<!-- source: modules/observability.md -->

# Observability

Metrics with a consistent identity, health probes that answer "can this pod serve" without turning a
shared outage into a fleet outage, correlation that propagates without exploding your time-series
storage, and an opt-in endpoint that tells you which platform capabilities a running service has.

## What you get

- **Common meter tags** — every meter carries `service` (= `spring.application.name`),
  `env` (= first active profile) and `platform.version` (from the platform jar manifest), so
  dashboards slice uniformly across the fleet.
- **Pod-local probes** — `/actuator/health/liveness` (`livenessState`) and
  `/actuator/health/readiness` (`readinessState`) exist everywhere, not only on Kubernetes. Neither
  checks an external system, so a database outage does not mark every replica unready at once.
- **A `dependencies` group** — `/actuator/health/dependencies` reports `db`, `rabbit` and `redis`
  **when present**, for dashboards and alerts.
- **Minimal exposure** — over http only `health`, `info` and `prometheus` are exposed. `metrics`,
  `platform` and everything else are an explicit opt-in.
- **`/actuator/platform` (opt-in)** — the `CapabilityDescriptor` report as JSON: which platform
  capabilities are ACTIVE in this running service, with provider detail. Generated services expose it.
- **Prometheus locally, OTLP when you have a collector** — the starter ships both metric registries
  and the OTLP span exporter; OTLP export is OFF by default because laptops have no collector.
  Zipkin is not supported: OpenTelemetry's Zipkin exporter is discontinued and fails against the OpenTelemetry the
  platform manages, so `platform-service-parent` refuses it at build time. Export over OTLP.
- **Bounded metric tags** — the trace ID never becomes a metric tag or observation key-value, and
  Boot's `uri` tag cap (`management.metrics.web.server.max-uri-tags` /
  `management.metrics.web.client.max-uri-tags`, default 100) stops a client that builds URIs by string
  concatenation (`"/orders/" + id`) from creating one series per ID. Prefer templates
  (`uri("/orders/{id}", id)`) anyway.

## Starter coordinates

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform</groupId>
  <artifactId>platform-starter-observability</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

## Zero-config behavior

An `EnvironmentPostProcessor` contributes management defaults through a lowest-precedence
property source named `platform-observability-defaults` (visible in `/actuator/env`):

| Contributed key | Value |
|---|---|
| `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include` | `health,info,prometheus` |
| `management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled` | `true` |
| `management.endpoint.health.group.liveness.include` | `livenessState` |
| `management.endpoint.health.group.readiness.include` | `readinessState` |
| `management.endpoint.health.group.dependencies.include` | `db,rabbit,redis` |
| `management.endpoint.health.validate-group-membership` | `false` (the dependencies list names optional members) |
| `management.tracing.baggage.remote-fields` | not set (was `X-Correlation-Id`; removed in the hardening phase 1) |
| `management.otlp.metrics.export.enabled` | `false` (only while `otlp.enabled=false`) |
| `management.tracing.export.otlp.enabled` | `false` (only while `otlp.enabled=false`) |

Any user-set value outranks every one of these. The top-level `/actuator/health` still aggregates every
contributor (the database included) — point probes at `readiness` and `liveness`, never at the top level.

> **Access:** 1.0.0 has no web security, so the exposed actuator endpoints answer anyone who can reach
> the application port. Phase 3 moves management to its own port, 8081 (ND13); until then, keep the
> application port off any public route.

## Properties

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `dc.platform.observability.enabled` | `true` | Kill switch for the whole capability. |
| `dc.platform.observability.common-tags.enabled` | `true` | Stamp `service`/`env`/`platform.version` on every meter. |
| `dc.platform.observability.otlp.enabled` | `false` | Enable OTLP export (metrics + traces). |
| `dc.platform.observability.health.groups.enabled` | `true` | Contribute liveness/readiness/dependencies group defaults. |
| `dc.platform.observability.platform-endpoint.enabled` | `true` | Serve `/actuator/platform` when it is exposed. |

(Hand-written until the generated reference lands in phase 14.)

## Exporting to a collector

Set `dc.platform.observability.otlp.enabled=true` and Boot's own export configuration takes
over — point it at your collector:

```yaml
dc.platform.observability.otlp.enabled: true
management:
  otlp:
    metrics:
      export:
        url: http://otel-collector:4318/v1/metrics
  opentelemetry:
    tracing:
      export:
        otlp:
          endpoint: http://otel-collector:4318/v1/traces
```

(`management.otlp.tracing.endpoint` was removed in Boot 4 — it no longer has any effect.)

## Sampling

Tracing is head-sampled: `management.tracing.sampling.probability`, Boot default `0.1`. The trace ID in
logs and error bodies does not depend on sampling — an unsampled request still has one. A head sampler
cannot know a request will fail, so **keeping every failed request's trace is the collector's job**: run
the OpenTelemetry Collector with tail sampling and an error policy.

```yaml
# OpenTelemetry Collector (contrib) — keep all errored traces, 10 % of the rest.
processors:
  tail_sampling:
    decision_wait: 10s
    policies:
      - name: errors
        type: status_code
        status_code: { status_codes: [ERROR] }
      - name: baseline
        type: probabilistic
        probabilistic: { sampling_percentage: 10 }
```

Tail sampling only sees spans the service exported, so with it in place set
`management.tracing.sampling.probability: 1.0` in the service and let the collector decide.

## Customize

- Define your own `MeterRegistryCustomizer` bean named `platformCommonTagsCustomizer` to replace
  the platform tags wholesale (any other bean name adds to them).
- Expose more endpoints: `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,info,prometheus,platform,metrics`.
- Override any contributed `management.*` key in `application.yml` — user config always wins.

## Replace / Disable

- `dc.platform.observability.platform-endpoint.enabled=false` removes `/actuator/platform`.
- A bean named `observabilityCapabilityDescriptor` replaces the banner/report entry.
- `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health` shrinks the http surface back to Boot's own.
- `dc.platform.observability.enabled=false` switches the capability off wholesale.

## Error codes

None — observability fails soft; a broken metrics/tracing setup must never take the service down.

## Testing

The `ApplicationContextRunner` matrix covers activation/back-off; `RANDOM_PORT` boot tests prove the
exposure and health-group defaults end to end (a simulated `db` outage leaves readiness UP and the
`dependencies` group DOWN), the scrape content, and Boot's client `uri` cap. The
EnvironmentPostProcessor is unit-tested against a `MockEnvironment` — user values always win.

## Local dev notes

`/actuator/prometheus` is live locally with the starter (scrape it, no collector needed). If a
management default is not taking effect, `/actuator/env` shows whether
`platform-observability-defaults` was outranked by your configuration.

<!-- source: modules/data.md -->

# Data / JPA

Tech-neutral persistence value objects (`platform-data-api`) plus opinionated Spring Data JPA
wiring (`platform-data-jpa-autoconfigure`): auditing, snake_case naming, sane Hibernate defaults,
a `Money` attribute converter, and a Flyway-presence guard — all on by default, all overridable.

## What you get

### `platform-data-api` (tech-neutral, no JPA on the classpath)

- **`Money`** — an immutable amount + ISO-4217 `Currency`. Same-currency `add`/`subtract` that fail
  loudly on a currency mismatch. Persisted to one column via the storage form
  `"<amount> <currencyCode>"` (`toStorageString()` / `parse(String)`) — the contract the JPA
  attribute converter implements.
- **`EntityId<T>`** — a typed wrapper around a raw id so an `OrderId` cannot be passed where a
  `CustomerId` is expected.
- **`PersistenceConventions`** — shared constants: `PHYSICAL_NAMING` (`snake_case`), standard column
  lengths (`CODE_LENGTH`, `NAME_LENGTH`, `DESCRIPTION_LENGTH`, `MONEY_LENGTH`, …), and the audit
  column names (`created_at`, `created_by`, `last_modified_at`, `last_modified_by`, `version`).

### `platform-data-jpa-autoconfigure` (opinionated Spring Data JPA)

- **Auditing** — `@CreatedDate`/`@CreatedBy`/`@LastModifiedDate`/`@LastModifiedBy` are populated
  automatically. The platform's auditor always records `"system"` (1.0.0 has no web security); to
  record a real caller, declare an `AuditorAware<String>` bean named `platformAuditorAware`.
- **Money / CorrelationId converters** — `MoneyConverter` and `CorrelationIdConverter` persist those
  value types to a single column. Opt in per field with `@Convert` (see below); they are not
  auto-applied (a library converter is not part of your scanned persistence unit, decision D34).
- **Hibernate defaults** — contributed as standard `spring.jpa.*` values at lowest precedence
  (source `platform-data-jpa-defaults`, visible in `/actuator/env`): `open-in-view=false`, batch
  size 50 with ordered inserts/updates, UTC jdbc time zone. snake_case physical naming is Boot's own
  default and is left in place (decision D35). Override any of these with the normal Boot keys.
- **Flyway guard** — startup fails fast if JPA is configured but migrations cannot run, with a message
  telling you to add the starter or set `dc.platform.data.jpa.require-migrations=false`. Spring Boot 4
  ships `FlywayAutoConfiguration` in `spring-boot-flyway`, so `flyway-core` alone is an engine nobody
  starts: the starter bundles both, and the guard checks both.
- **Bounded waits (D110)** — in the same `platform-data-jpa-defaults` source:
  - `spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout=5000`: a request behind an exhausted pool fails in 5 s
    (Hikari's own 30 s lets request threads pile up) with a 503 `DC-DATA-0503`;
  - `spring.transaction.default-timeout=30s`: every transaction, Spring Data repository methods
    included; once it is spent the driver cancels the running statement (reliably for plain SQL; for SQL
    running inside a PL/SQL function the cancel is best-effort, and was once missed in testing);
  - `spring.jpa.properties.jakarta.persistence.query.timeout=30000` and
    `spring.jdbc.template.query-timeout=30s`: a query that runs **outside** a transaction is bounded
    too. A declared repository query (`@Query` or a derived `findBy…`) has no transaction of its own,
    and neither has a service method without `@Transactional`. Inside a transaction the remaining
    transaction time is used instead for repository queries and for queries created on the injected
    `EntityManager` (or its unwrapped `Session`'s `createQuery`/`createNativeQuery`). Two paths bypass that
    and take this default instead — past a shorter transaction's deadline, or cutting a longer one short:
    Hibernate's `Session.createSelectionQuery(…)` and a query on the raw `getDelegate()`. On those, set the
    timeout on the query yourself (`.setTimeout(seconds)`). `EntityManager.find` outside a transaction is
    not a query; only the read timeout below bounds it;
  - on a pool whose URL is `jdbc:oracle:`, the driver's `oracle.jdbc.ReadTimeout` (the backstop for what
    a cancel cannot stop: a PL/SQL or lock wait, a dead network) and `oracle.net.CONNECT_TIMEOUT=10000` are
    added to the pool's `data-source-properties`. The read timeout is
    `dc.platform.data.jpa.oracle.read-timeout` (default `60s`). It bounds **each wait for the database's
    answer**, so a statement the database takes longer than that to answer (a long update, an index build,
    a lock wait) fails whatever its transaction timeout: a service with `@Transactional(timeout = 300)`
    batch work raises it to match. Flyway's own connection, when migrations run as a separate user (see
    *Schema owner and runtime user*), gets the connect timeout and
    `dc.platform.data.jpa.oracle.flyway-read-timeout` (default `10m`), so a long migration statement (an
    index build) can finish while a database that stops answering still fails startup. Migrations that run
    through the pool (no separate Flyway user) get the pool's value. The connect timeout covers only the
    TCP connect: a database that accepts the connection and then never answers is ended by the read timeout
    (measured: a silent peer at startup failed after 610 s with a separate Flyway user, `ORA-17002 … Socket
    read timed out`). A shorter startup probe restarts the service first, which also bounds it; lower
    `flyway-read-timeout` if a faster, clearer failure matters more than long migration statements; A pool you build and start yourself (`new HikariDataSource(config)`) is sealed, so
    nothing is added to it: set both properties on its config;
  - `leak-detection-threshold=20000` (a stack trace for a connection held over 20 s) only under the
    `local` profile, and never when `prod` is active as well.
  Hikari's keepalive (2 min) and max lifetime (30 min) are its own defaults. Set any key yourself to
  change it — a value you set always wins (for the driver timeouts: a `data-source-properties` entry or
  a JVM system property).
- **Data errors as problems (D111)** — handled by the errors capability: a unique, foreign-key, NOT
  NULL or check violation is a 409 `DC-DATA-0409` (Hibernate's own null check included), a concurrent
  update or lock a 409 `DC-DATA-0410`, an unavailable database or a timeout a retryable 503
  `DC-DATA-0503` (a transaction whose deadline passed before a flush or commit included, and a rollback
  that fails because the connection broke, e.g. after the driver read timeout). A connection lost while
  **committing** is a non-retryable 500 whatever its cause, because the outcome is unknown (recognised for
  Spring's imperative transaction managers such as `JpaTransactionManager`, not reactive ones; HI-0071). The body never names SQL, tables or
  constraints; the platform logs the full exception once, at WARN on the request's trace. Hibernate logs the
  failed statement's error code and driver message as two WARN lines of its own just before (logger
  `org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.error`); they are the only record when application code catches the exception, so
  the platform leaves them on — set `logging.level.org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.error=error` to drop them. This
  also covers raw Hibernate/JPA exceptions from code that uses the `EntityManager` directly (Spring
  translates only behind a repository).

## Transactions

- Put `@Transactional` on the service method that owns the unit of work, and
  `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` on service methods that only read. Spring Data's inherited
  repository methods (`findAll`, `save`, …) already run in a transaction (read-only for reads);
  a declared query method does not, unless you annotate it or call it from a transactional service.
- A runtime exception thrown out of a `@Transactional` method rolls the transaction back. A
  **checked** exception does not: Spring commits by default. Declare
  `@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)` where a checked exception must undo the work.
  Both verified against Oracle (`OracleTransactionRulesIT`).

## Migrations

`platform-starter-data-jpa` runs Flyway at startup from `classpath:db/migration`; Hibernate DDL stays off
once Flyway is present (never set `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create/update` in production). The
service archetype's `data` feature ships `db/migration/V1__create_note.sql` for its `Note` sample and a
`NoteRepositoryTest` that proves the migrated schema with CRUD across transactions, rollback, and a
NOT NULL violation on H2. H2 covers local runs and tests only — the generated `prod` profile disables
the embedded fallback.

Flyway's safe settings are pinned (D112), so an upgrade cannot loosen them: `clean-disabled=true`,
`validate-on-migrate=true`, `out-of-order=false`, `validate-migration-naming=true`. In practice:
- name every file `V<version>__<description>.sql` (two underscores) — a misnamed file fails startup
  instead of being skipped;
- never edit an applied migration — the checksum mismatch blocks startup; add `V<next>__…` instead;
- out-of-order migrations are refused outside the `local` profile, with a startup diagnostic that
  names the fix, however they were switched on (`spring.flyway.*`, `flyway.conf`, any customizer): the
  check runs on Flyway's finished configuration, before anything migrates.

### Schema owner and runtime user

In production, migrations and the application connect as different database users:

| User | Grants | Configured by |
|---|---|---|
| Schema owner (e.g. `APP_OWNER`) | owns the tables; `create table/sequence/view/procedure` | `spring.flyway.user` / `spring.flyway.password` — Flyway only |
| Runtime user (e.g. `APP_RUNTIME`) | `create session` and `select/insert/update/delete` on the owner's tables, `select` on its sequences; **no** `alter`, `drop` or `create` | `spring.datasource.username` / `password` — the pool |

The runtime user resolves the owner's unqualified table names either per session —
`spring.datasource.hikari.connection-init-sql=ALTER SESSION SET CURRENT_SCHEMA=APP_OWNER` — or through
synonyms the owner creates. Grants for tables added by a later migration go in that migration (or a
repeatable `R__grants.sql`), so a deploy never needs a manual step.

With `spring.flyway.user` set, Boot gives Flyway its own connection outside the pool; the platform adds
the connect timeout and `flyway-read-timeout` (10 min) to it. One exception: a `{vendor}` placeholder in
`spring.flyway.locations` makes Boot open one connection to detect the database **before** the platform
can set them. Keep the default `db/migration` location, or set the driver properties on the JVM, e.g.
`-Doracle.net.CONNECT_TIMEOUT=10000 -Doracle.jdbc.ReadTimeout=600000`. A JVM system property applies to
every Oracle connection and wins over both platform values, so the pool then gets the same read timeout:
choose it for the longest statement either side runs. The same JVM properties are the way for a `Flyway` bean you define yourself
with a URL (`Flyway.configure().dataSource(url, user, password)`): Flyway then builds its own connection,
which the platform does not touch.

## Oracle

Production runs Oracle 19c; Oracle is the only certified database (PostgreSQL is out for now). Use the
Oracle starter — it brings the JDBC driver **and** `flyway-database-oracle` (Flyway 10+ refuses a
database without its module: `Unsupported Database`):

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform</groupId>
  <artifactId>platform-starter-data-jpa-oracle</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

Generate a new service with `-Dfeatures=data -Ddatabase=oracle`; H2 still backs its local runs and tests.

Behaviour verified against Oracle with Hibernate in 19c mode (`@Tag("docker")` tests in
`platform-data-jpa-autoconfigure`):

| Topic | What to do |
|---|---|
| Names | Unquoted snake_case names are stored upper-case; identifiers are limited to 128 characters (ORA-00972 beyond). |
| Keys | Sequences: `allocationSize` must equal the sequence's `INCREMENT BY`. Identity columns (`generated by default as identity`) work too. |
| `boolean` | Stored as `NUMBER(1)`; 19c has no SQL `BOOLEAN` — never use it in a migration. |
| `Instant` | Map to `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` (D114). Hibernate reads `Instant` as an offset date-time; a plain `TIMESTAMP` column fails on read with ORA-18716. Values are unchanged across JVM and session time zones. |
| Paging | `Pageable` becomes `OFFSET … FETCH`; always sort for stable pages. |
| Empty strings | Oracle stores `''` as `NULL`: a `NOT NULL` column rejects an empty string (409 `DC-DATA-0409`). |
| Migrations | Write them 19c-safe: no `BOOLEAN`, no `IF [NOT] EXISTS`, `FROM DUAL` in selects, end PL/SQL blocks with a `/` line. |

The certification container is Oracle 23ai Free (no 19c image exists): Hibernate is pinned to 19 there,
but hand-written SQL runs against 23ai, which accepts 19c-invalid syntax — review migrations for 19c.
RAC failover (FCF/ONS, Application Continuity) is not covered.

## Starter coordinates

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform</groupId>
  <artifactId>platform-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

## Properties

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `dc.platform.data.jpa.enabled` | `true` | Kill switch for the JPA capability. |
| `dc.platform.data.jpa.require-migrations` | `true` | Fail startup when JPA is present but Flyway is absent. |

## Persisting Money / CorrelationId

```java
@Convert(converter = MoneyConverter.class)
private Money price;                 // stored as "19.99 AED"

@Convert(converter = CorrelationIdConverter.class)
private CorrelationId correlationId; // stored as 32 hex chars
```

## Using the value types

```java
@Column(name = "reference_code", length = PersistenceConventions.CODE_LENGTH)
private String referenceCode;

Money price = Money.of("19.99", "AED");
Money total = price.add(Money.of("1.00", "AED"));   // 20.99 AED
```

## Local dev notes

`platform-data-api` has no datastore dependency at all. The JPA slice tests against H2; no
Docker or network is required for the default build. The Oracle tests run under `mvn -Pdocker verify`;
a cold Oracle container copies about 3 GB of datafiles (minutes on a laptop disk), so set
`testcontainers.reuse.enable=true` in `~/.testcontainers.properties` to keep the instance warm between
runs (each run still gets a fresh schema user).
