<!-- source: modules/messaging.md -->

# Messaging

Publish and handle integration events without coupling application code to a broker: inject
`EventPublisher`, mark handler methods `@EventHandler`, and pick the transport (in-memory for tests,
RabbitMQ for real) via a starter.

> **RabbitMQ only.** The Kafka transport was removed (Spring-native plan v2, ND10). Phase 6 of the
> [plan](../spring-native/plan.md) moves this capability to Spring AMQP (`RabbitTemplate`,
> `@RabbitListener`); this page describes the current API until then.

## What you get

- **`EventPublisher`** — `publish(destination, event)` / `publish(destination, payload)`.
  AT-LEAST-ONCE, blocks until the transport acknowledges the send.
- **`EventEnvelope<T>`** — immutable envelope; `eventType`/`eventVersion` are derived from
  `@EventType` on the payload class, or fall back to the simple class name / version 1.
- **`@EventHandler(destination, eventType)`** — marks a method as a handler; takes either the
  payload type or `EventEnvelope<T>` when headers/metadata are needed.
- **Structured headers** — every message carries `eventId`, `eventType`, `eventVersion`, `producer`, and
  `traceparent` when a trace is active. A credential-named header is refused. A handler runs in a span continuing
  the message's trace.
- **Bounded retry + DLQ** — a failed handler is retried up to `handler.retry.max-attempts`, with a capped exponential
  backoff, then dead-lettered: by the broker on RabbitMQ, by a republish to `destination + dlq.suffix` elsewhere. A payload
  that cannot be read, or a newer version than the handler knows, goes there on the first attempt.
- **Metrics** — `platform.messaging.published` (publish outcome) and `platform.messaging.handled`
  (handler outcome: success/retry/dlq), both via Micrometer when a `MeterRegistry` is present.
- **`/actuator/platform`** reports `messaging[ACTIVE <provider>]`, or `INACTIVE` when no single
  `EventTransport` bean is configured.

For a publish tied to a database change, use the [transactional outbox](outbox.md): `EventPublisher` sends immediately,
so a crash right after your commit loses the event.

Delivery is at-least-once: every message carries a stable `eventId` header, generated once when the envelope is built, and
consumers deduplicate by it. On RabbitMQ a send waits for the broker's publisher confirm; an unroutable message, a nack or
no confirm within `dc.platform.messaging.rabbit.confirm-timeout` (default `5s`) throws `EventPublishException`, so **a
destination needs a bound queue before you publish to it**.

## Starter coordinates

Pick exactly one (each brings its own `EventTransport`):

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform</groupId>
  <artifactId>platform-starter-messaging-inmemory</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform</groupId>
  <artifactId>platform-starter-messaging-rabbit</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

## Zero-config behavior

```java snippet:messaging-usage
@EventType("OrderPlaced")
record OrderPlaced(String orderId) {}

@Service
class OrdersService {
    private final EventPublisher publisher;

    OrdersService(EventPublisher publisher) {
        this.publisher = publisher;
    }

    void place(String orderId) {
        publisher.publish("dc.orders", new OrderPlaced(orderId));
    }
}

@Component
class OrdersEventHandlers {
    @EventHandler(destination = "dc.orders", eventType = "OrderPlaced")
    void onOrderPlaced(OrderPlaced event) {
        // ...
    }
}
```

## Properties

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `dc.platform.messaging.enabled` | `true` | Kill switch for the whole capability. |
| `dc.platform.messaging.default-destination-prefix` | `dc.` | Naming convention only; not enforced. |
| `dc.platform.messaging.handler.retry.max-attempts` | `3` | Total attempts before a handler failure is dead-lettered. |
| `dc.platform.messaging.handler.retry.backoff` | `1s` | Pause before the second attempt; doubles per attempt. |
| `dc.platform.messaging.handler.retry.max-backoff` | `30s` | The longest pause between attempts. |
| `dc.platform.messaging.dlq.suffix` | `.dlq` | The DLQ destination on transports without native dead-lettering. |
| `dc.platform.messaging.rabbit.quorum-queues` | `true` | Declare quorum queues, main and dead-letter; `false` for classic. An existing queue of the other type fails its declaration: RabbitMQ does not convert queues. |
| `dc.platform.messaging.rabbit.confirm-timeout` | `5s` | How long a send waits for the broker's confirm. |
| `dc.platform.messaging.rabbit.prefetch` | `10` | Messages a consumer holds at once, and so how many a retrying handler can delay. |
| `dc.platform.messaging.rabbit.shutdown-timeout` | `30s` | How long a stopping consumer waits for the handler in flight. Shutdown phases run in turn: with the defaults, keep the pod's grace period above about 95 s (web drain 30 s, outbox `stop-timeout` 30 s and its joins, this). |
| `dc.platform.messaging.rabbit.delivery-limit` | `20` | Returns a quorum queue allows before dead-lettering a message that keeps killing its consumer. A message merely held by a stopping consumer counts too, hence well above what rolling restarts reach. |

(Hand-written until the generated reference lands in phase 14.)

### RabbitMQ: destination syntax

Destinations are `"exchange"` (empty routing key) or `"exchange:routingKey"`, e.g.
`"dc.orders:order.placed"`. Each subscription declares a durable topic exchange, a bound queue
`<exchange>.<routingKey>.<group>` and a dead-letter exchange + queue `….dlq`. Declarations run on every new connection, so a
service starts without the broker, and a broker that lost its definitions gets them back.

### RabbitMQ: how a delivery ends

The container acks after the handler returns, including any transaction the handler ran.

| Outcome | What happens |
|---|---|
| Handler returns | Acked |
| Handler keeps failing | `max-attempts` attempts in the consumer, then the broker dead-letters it. With the defaults, 3 s of backoff plus the handler's own time per poison message; other messages the consumer holds wait |
| Unreadable payload, or a version newer than `@EventType` declares | The DLQ at once, with a WARN or ERROR that never quotes the payload. A replay delivers a newer version after upgrading |
| Consumer stops | The handler in flight finishes, within `shutdown-timeout`; buffered messages go back; a retry backoff stops and puts its message back |
| Consumer dies mid-handler | The broker redelivers; `delivery-limit` dead-letters a message that keeps doing this |

Quorum queues dead-letter at-least-once (RabbitMQ 3.10 or later); classic queues do so at-most-once.

Handler time is yours to bound: a handler that blocks holds its consumer and the messages it has buffered. Give it timeouts, as the
data capability's transaction default does. Handlers belong on singletons created at startup: a bean with a handler created once
consumers have started fails with an error, since a running consumer could already have acknowledged what it should receive.

Consumers start before the outbox's drainer and stop after it, so a drained event finds its consumers. So a lifecycle bean a handler
depends on needs a lower phase than `DEFAULT_PHASE - 8192`, or the handler can run before it starts and after it stops.

Handlers on one destination share a queue: each message goes to the handler declaring its `eventType`, else to one declaring none.
Two handlers that could receive the same message fail startup. A message no handler wants is acknowledged and counted as
`outcome=ignored`.

**Guarantees, and what they are not.** Delivery is at-least-once and unordered. **Deduplicate by `eventId`:** insert it in a
processed-events table with a unique constraint, in the same transaction as the business write, and skip on a violation.
`docs/samples/rabbitmq-messaging/` shows it. Use `OutboxPublisher` for any publish tied to a database change; a direct
`EventPublisher.publish` fails if the broker is down or the message is unroutable, and the caller must handle that.

**Schema rule.** Consumers tolerate unknown fields, so adding a field needs no version change. A change an old consumer cannot
read raises `@EventType(version = …)`.

### RabbitMQ: inspecting and replaying a DLQ

`tooling/scripts/rabbit-dlq-replay.py inspect <queue>` prints headers and leaves the messages there; `replay <queue>` moves what
is in the DLQ now back to the main queue, keeping event ids. It needs the `rabbitmq_shovel` and `rabbitmq_shovel_management`
plugins. Fix the cause first, or the messages come straight back. Do not delete the main queue during a replay: the shovel would
publish into nothing.

## Customize

Provide your own `EventSerializer` bean to replace the default Jackson JSON codec:

```java
@Bean
EventSerializer avroEventSerializer() {
    return new AvroEventSerializer();
}
```

## Replace / Disable

- Define your own `EventPublisher` bean to replace the default entirely.
- Define your own `EventTransport` bean to use a provider the platform doesn't ship yet.
- `dc.platform.messaging.enabled=false` switches the capability off wholesale.

## Testing

Use `platform-starter-messaging-inmemory` in tests regardless of your production provider:
`InMemoryEventTransport.awaitIdle(Duration)` gives sleep-free, deterministic publish/handle
assertions. `platform-messaging-test`'s `TestEventTransport` and `@AutoConfigureTestTransport` are
purpose-built for this.

## Local dev notes

The in-memory provider needs no Docker or network. RabbitMQ round-trip tests are
`@Tag("docker")` (Testcontainers) and excluded from the default build; run them with
`mvn -Pdocker -pl messaging/platform-messaging-rabbit -am verify`
against a running Docker daemon, or start `docker-compose.local.yml` for manual exploration.

<!-- source: modules/outbox.md -->

# Transactional Outbox

**Guaranteed publish alongside a database change.** The event is written to a table in the same transaction as your
business write, so both commit or neither does. A separate drainer then delivers it, at least once. A crash between
the commit and the send loses nothing.

Use it for any publish tied to a database change. `EventPublisher` sends immediately and cannot give that guarantee.

The outbox is a messaging-durability mechanism, not an audit mechanism.

## Add it to a service

1. **Add the starter**, next to a transport starter and your data starter:

   ```xml
   <dependency>
     <groupId>ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform</groupId>
     <artifactId>platform-starter-messaging-outbox</artifactId>
   </dependency>
   <dependency>
     <groupId>ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform</groupId>
     <artifactId>platform-starter-messaging-rabbit</artifactId>
   </dependency>
   ```

2. **Add the table to your migrations.** Copy
   `classpath:ae/gov/dubaicustoms/platform/messaging/outbox/platform_outbox.sql` (in `platform-messaging-outbox`) into
   your own sequence, for example `V7__platform_outbox.sql`. With a separate runtime user, also grant it `select, insert,
   update, delete` on the table. The platform never creates the table: a runtime user has no DDL rights, and a migration
   inside a platform jar would collide with your version numbers. If the table is missing, startup fails and names this
   file.

3. **Publish inside your transaction:**

   ```java
   @Transactional
   public void place(Order order) {
       orders.save(order);
       outbox.publish("dc.orders:order.placed", EventEnvelope.of(new OrderPlaced(order.id())).key(order.id()).build());
   }
   ```

No dependency on JPA: it needs a `DataSource`, and joins your transaction under `JpaTransactionManager` or
`DataSourceTransactionManager`.

## What it guarantees, and what it does not

| Guarantee | Detail |
|---|---|
| Atomic with the business write | A rollback leaves no row. `publish` **throws** if no transaction owns a connection of the outbox's `DataSource`, or anywhere under an `afterCommit` callback, where nothing would commit the row. Use one transaction manager per outbox database: with a second one, a pool set to `auto-commit=false` and a read through the outbox's `DataSource` inside the other manager's transaction, the check cannot tell |
| At-least-once delivery | A kill between a send and its commit repeats the rows of that batch: at most `batch-size` duplicates per kill |
| Stable event id | Generated once, when the envelope is built; the same on every retry, sent as header `eventId` |
| Acknowledged sends | A row is marked sent only after the transport acknowledges it. On RabbitMQ that is a publisher confirm; unroutable or nacked messages fail |

| Not offered | Consequence for you |
|---|---|
| Exactly-once | **Consumers must deduplicate by `eventId`** |
| Ordering | Retries and `SKIP LOCKED` reorder events, even for one key. Consumers must tolerate a later event arriving first |

Stored rows: headers named like a credential (`*token`, `*password`, `*pwd`, `authorization`, `*cookie`…) are refused with
an exception, and of the propagated context only `traceparent` and `tracestate` are stored. The principal is the subject id only. `last_error` holds the exception class only. **The payload is your
data and is stored as is**, so do not put tokens or personal data in an event you would not want in this table.

## How it works

The drainer runs on **its own small connection pool** (`pool-size`, default 2), so a stuck or backlogged drainer cannot
starve request threads. It takes the URL, credentials, driver properties and `connection-init-sql` of your URL-configured
pool (not its size, timeouts or auto-commit) and adds the Oracle read and connect bounds itself. Those credentials are read
once: rotating them on your pool needs a restart. If your `DataSource` is anything else, including a Hikari pool configured
with `dataSource` or `dataSourceClassName`, startup fails rather than risk wrapping a pool or reading another database:
define an `OutboxConnections` bean with a small pool of its own. A routing RabbitMQ `ConnectionFactory` is not supported.

Each batch is one transaction: claim due rows with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, send each, record each, commit. Row locks
keep other instances off those rows, and the database releases them when a pod dies, so there is no lease and no recovery
job. A long-running send holds its row locks and one drainer connection, not a request thread.

| Failure | What happens |
|---|---|
| Sink down or slow (no confirm in time) | The row is retried with backoff and the drainer pauses (up to `max-backoff`). **It never parks**: recovery delivers the whole backlog |
| Sink rejects the message (unroutable, no such exchange) | Counts toward `max-rejections`, then the row is `PARKED` with a WARN and a metric. Other rows keep flowing |
| Database down | The batch rolls back and the drainer retries with the same pause |
| A row's stored headers cannot be read | Parked at once; the rest of the batch continues |
| Shutdown | The batch ends after the send in flight and commits what was sent; idle waits end immediately |
| Custom transport | Throw `EventPublishException` with `rejected=true` when the sink refuses a message; any other exception is treated as an outage and never parks |

## Parked rows

Parked rows are never deleted automatically. Find out why (`last_error`, the WARN line), fix the cause (usually a missing
queue binding), then replay; the event keeps its id:

```sql
update platform_outbox
   set status = 'PENDING', rejections = 0, next_attempt_at = current_timestamp
 where status = 'PARKED'
   and destination = :destination;
```

## Properties

All under `dc.platform.messaging.outbox`.

| Property | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `true` | `false` publishes after commit, **no longer guaranteed**, and logs a startup WARN saying so |
| `pool-size` | `2` | The most connections the drainer holds, on its own pool. At least 2: one for batches, one for metrics and retention |
| `batch-size` | `50` | The most rows per transaction, and so the most duplicates a kill can cause |
| `poll-interval` | `1s` | The pause when nothing is due |
| `max-rejections` | `10` | Rejections by the sink before a row is parked; outages do not count |
| `initial-backoff` | `1s` | First per-row retry delay; doubles per attempt |
| `max-backoff` | `5m` | Longest per-row retry delay and longest pause after a failure |
| `sent-retention` | `24h` | How long a sent row is kept; deleted in bounded batches |
| `statement-timeout` | `30s` | The timeout on each drainer statement |
| `gauge-interval` | `5s` | How often the backlog metrics refresh (on the drainer's thread, never on scrape) |
| `retention-interval` | `5m` | How often sent rows are deleted |
| `stop-timeout` | `30s` | How long a shutdown waits for the batch in flight |
| `read-timeout` | `60s` | The Oracle driver's read timeout on the drainer's connections, unless your pool sets one |

## Metrics

| Meter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `platform.outbox.pending` | Rows waiting to be sent |
| `platform.outbox.oldest.pending.age` | Age in seconds of the oldest waiting row: the drain lag. **Alert on this** |
| `platform.outbox.parked` | Parked rows. **Alert on anything above 0** |
| `platform.outbox.drainer.running` | 1 while the drainer's thread is alive. **Alert on 0** |
| `platform.outbox.gauges.age` | Seconds since the backlog figures last refreshed; high means they are stale, typically a database outage |
| `platform.outbox.sent`, `.failed`, `.parkings` | Counters. No tags, so no event ids or destinations in labels |
| `hikaricp_*{pool="platform-outbox"}` | The drainer's own pool |

## Limits worth knowing

- **Outbox off or absent, inside an `afterCommit` callback.** Without a guarantee to protect, the fallback paths are best
  effort there. With the outbox off, a publish in an `afterCommit` callback goes out at once, even if a `REQUIRES_NEW`
  transaction around it later rolls back. In the relay's fallback, a `REQUIRED` transaction opened in such a callback joins
  the finished one, as Spring warns, and its dispatch never runs. The outbox itself refuses in all these shapes.

## Replace / disable

- Define your own `OutboxPublisher`, `OutboxContext`, `OutboxDrainer` or `outboxCapabilityDescriptor` bean to replace
  the default.
- `dc.platform.messaging.outbox.enabled=false` keeps application code working, with publishes after commit. A crash
  between the commit and the send then loses the event.

<!-- source: modules/dx.md -->

# Developer Experience (archetype · upgrade-check · conformance · golden path)

The DX tooling turns "assemble a service by hand from a dozen starters and rediscover every
convention" into a one-command generate-and-go, and keeps generated services on the platform's rails.

## Service archetype (`tooling/platform-service-archetype`)

A `maven-archetype` that generates a ready-to-run service. See [quickstart](../quickstart.md) for the
generate command. Properties:

| Property | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `platformVersion` | the archetype's own version (stamped at build time by resource filtering) | platform version the service builds against (parent + BOM) |
| `features` | `none` | `none` or a comma-separated subset of `messaging`, `data`, `restclient` (no spaces or duplicates) — adds starters, sample code, and sample tests |

Feature tokens are matched exactly; any other value fails generation with `unsupported features value`
(batch-mode `archetype:generate` ignores `<validationRegex>`, so the check lives in the `pom.xml`
template). Structured logging is part of every service, not a feature.

The generated project ships `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md` (so coding agents use platform APIs instead of
vanilla Spring), a `PlatformConformanceTest`, platform slice tests, real-HTTP tests
(`SecurityIntegrationTest` with a loopback JWKS issuer, `StructuredLoggingTest` parsing the emitted JSON
events), per-feature tests (`data/NoteRepositoryTest`, `client/GreetingClientTest`), and a
profile-aware `application.yml`: offline placeholders apply to every profile except `prod`, and `prod`
fails fast when the IdP, datasource, or downstream base URL is missing. Feature samples are
conditional: when a feature is off, its sample sources render empty (Velocity `#if`) and its starter
is omitted.

The archetype is also checked Maven-natively by `mvn -Parchetype-it -pl tooling/platform-service-archetype
verify`, which generates `basic` (every optional property omitted), `service` (`data,restclient`), and
`full` (all features, relocated package, hyphenated artifactId) and runs `verify` on each. That profile
is off by default (it needs the platform installed first); the default reactor build never runs it.

## Consumer conformance rules (`PlatformUsageRules`)

`ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform.test.arch.PlatformUsageRules.all()` (in `platform-test-api`) is a set of
ArchUnit rules a service runs over its own production classes via the generated
`PlatformConformanceTest`. Each failure names the platform alternative:

| Rule | Banned | Use instead |
|---|---|---|
| `noDirectMessagingInfrastructure` | `RabbitTemplate` / RabbitMQ listener containers | `EventPublisher` / `@EventHandler` |
| `noHandRolledExceptionHandler` | `@RestControllerAdvice extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler` | throw `PlatformException` subtypes |
| `noSystemGetenv` | `System.getenv(...)` | Spring config placeholders (`${...}`, populated by Spring Cloud Vault) |

Rules match banned types by fully-qualified name, so a service that does not pull in Rabbit
still compiles the test.

**Escape hatch (discouraged):** a team with a documented reason may delete `PlatformConformanceTest`
from its service. The rules teach the platform way — deleting them silences that guidance.

## `upgrade-check` goal

Reports what changes when a service moves to a new platform version, without touching sources:

```bash
mvn ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform:platform-build-maven-plugin:upgrade-check -Dplatform.target=<version>
```

It resolves the target `platform-bom` and diffs its managed versions against the project's current
ones, and scans the project's `application*.{yml,yaml,properties}` for keys deprecated in the target
version (read from the target platform jars' `spring-configuration-metadata.json`). Output: a console
summary plus `target/platform-upgrade-report.md` linking the train release notes. v1 scope is version
diff + property deprecation scan; binary-compatibility (japicmp) checks are future work.

## Golden path (`tooling/scripts/golden-path.sh`)

The executable DX contract, run by the CI `generator-gate` job:

1. install the platform (tests skipped; the `build` job is the tested gate) into an **isolated** Maven
   repository (`GP_MAVEN_REPO`, default a fresh one) and record the installed archetype;
2. check that invalid `features` values are rejected;
3. for all 8 combinations of `messaging`/`data`/`restclient` — one with every optional property
   omitted, one relocated into a directory with a space — generate **outside the checkout**, assert the
   generated files, run the generated `mvn verify` (every expected test class must run, none skipped),
   check the repackaged jar, boot it with `java -jar` on a free port and probe readiness, the capability
   report (present *and* absent capabilities), 401 for missing/untrusted/expired/malformed tokens, 200
   for a token from the loopback JWKS issuer, correlation echo, and the JSON log contract;
4. for `data,restclient`: `mvn spring-boot:run`, the `local` profile, `prod` with each mandatory
   setting missing (must refuse to start), and `prod` with supplied settings booted twice on one file
   database.

Each service must finish generate → verify → packaged boot within a 10-minute SLA (`GP_SLA_SECONDS`).
Owned processes are killed on exit; the work directory and evidence (`GP_EVIDENCE`) are kept on failure.
It uses `maven-archetype-plugin:3.1.2` (the documented version; 3.4.0 generates project-less on Maven
3.9.x too). The archetype must not use `archetype-post-generate.groovy`: 3.4.0's Groovy cannot parse
Java 25 class files, so feature pruning stays in Velocity.

<!-- source: modules/openapi.md -->

# OpenAPI

> **Coming in iteration 2.** This capability is parked: it is built and tested in the repository but not released in 1.0.0, not in the BOM and not offered by the archetype. Iteration 2 of the [Spring-native plan](../spring-native/plan.md) reworks it (Phase 8, as part of the REST API); this page describes the pre-rework design.

A springdoc-generated OpenAPI document that already knows how the platform reports errors, so no
team hand-writes the same 4xx/5xx shapes.

## What you get

- **`/v3/api-docs`** and **`/swagger-ui.html`** — springdoc's usual surface, zero controller
  annotations required to get a baseline document.
- **Title/version identity for free** — default to `spring.application.name` /
  `info.app.version` (falls back further to `dev`); override explicitly when you want a
  human-facing title that differs from the Spring application name.
- **Bearer-JWT security scheme documented by default** — matches the platform's expected auth
  model; every operation is marked as requiring it (turn off per-operation as usual, or switch
  the scheme off platform-wide).
- **Every operation documents the platform's error shape** — `ProblemDetail` schema plus default
  400/401/403/404/409/422/500 responses appended automatically (errors slice, phase 4); an
  operation-defined status is never overwritten.

## Starter coordinates

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform</groupId>
  <artifactId>platform-starter-openapi</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

## Properties

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `dc.platform.openapi.enabled` | `true` | Kill switch for the whole capability. |
| `dc.platform.openapi.title` | `""` (→ `spring.application.name`) | Document title. |
| `dc.platform.openapi.version` | `""` (→ `info.app.version`, then `dev`) | Document version. |
| `dc.platform.openapi.security-scheme` | `BEARER_JWT` | `BEARER_JWT` or `NONE`. |

(Hand-written until the generated reference lands in phase 14.)

## Customize

- Define your own `OpenAPI` bean to replace the platform default wholesale (title, servers,
  security schemes — everything).
- Contribute additional `OpenApiCustomizer` beans (a different bean name) to layer more
  documentation on top; the platform's `platformProblemDetailOpenApiCustomizer` still runs.
- `dc.platform.openapi.security-scheme=NONE` documents no authentication (public APIs).

## Replace / Disable

- `springdoc.api-docs.enabled=false` / `springdoc.swagger-ui.enabled=false` turn off springdoc's
  own endpoints (Boot property, not a platform one).
- `dc.platform.openapi.enabled=false` switches the platform layer off; springdoc still generates
  a document from your own beans/annotations if the starter is on the classpath.

## Error codes

None — the OpenAPI document is generated at request time; a malformed customizer only affects
that document, never request handling.

## Testing

The `ApplicationContextRunner` matrix covers activation/back-off/title-version resolution/
security-scheme toggling; `ProblemDetailOpenApiCustomizerTest` unit-tests the schema/response
appending directly; a `RANDOM_PORT` boot test asserts `/v3/api-docs` contains both the
`ProblemDetail` schema and the `bearer-jwt` scheme end to end.

## Local dev notes

Open `http://localhost:<port>/swagger-ui.html` while the service is running. If a status code is
missing from an operation's documented responses, check whether the controller method already
declares that status explicitly — the platform customizer never overwrites an existing entry.

<!-- source: modules/restclient.md -->

# REST Client

> **Coming in iteration 2.** This capability is parked: it is built and tested in the repository but not released in 1.0.0, not in the BOM and not offered by the archetype. Iteration 2 of the [Spring-native plan](../spring-native/plan.md) reworks it (Phase 9); this page describes the pre-rework design.

Platform-conventional outbound REST calls: inject `PlatformRestClientFactory` instead of
`RestClient.Builder` to get W3C trace propagation, timeouts and a deadline, safe retries, a circuit
breaker, a bulkhead and one failure type on every outbound call.

## What you get

- **`PlatformRestClientFactory`** — `builder(String clientName)` returns a pre-configured
  `RestClient.Builder` on the JDK `HttpClient` request factory.
- **Trace propagation** — every client is instrumented with the observation registry, so the
  current trace travels as the standard `traceparent` header (the platform's only correlation id).
  No custom correlation header is sent or read (the former `X-Correlation-Id` behaviour is gone).
- **Per-client settings** — everything below has a default, overridable per client name.
- **One failure type** — every failure throws `RemoteCallException`; `kind()` says which (see below).
  At most 8 KiB of an error body is read. The 1KB snippet has common credential forms removed: authorization and
  cookie lines, auth schemes, JWTs, and secret-named values in JSON and forms; a body with a secret-named XML element
  loses its whole snippet. This is best effort, by pattern:
  an encoded or oddly named secret, or personal or business data, can remain. It also errs the safe way, so
  "basic validation failed" loses a word. Treat `bodySnippet()` as untrusted: never return it to your own callers.
  `remoteCorrelationId()` is deprecated and always empty for platform-created exceptions:
  caller and callee share one trace, so the caller's own `traceId` joins both sides' logs.
- **Retries, deadline, breaker, bulkhead** — see [Resilience](#resilience).
- **`PlatformRestClientCustomizer` extension point** — ordered beans that further customize a
  named client's builder.
- **Observations** — every call records an `http.client.requests` observation (metrics/tracing via
  the application's `ObservationRegistry`), tagged `client.name=<clientName>`.
- **No token relay** — the caller's bearer token is never forwarded (removed in Spring-native Phase 1).
  Iteration 2 adds basic auth and OAuth client credentials for outbound calls.

## Starter coordinates

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform</groupId>
  <artifactId>platform-starter-restclient</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

## Zero-config behavior

```java
@Service
class OrdersClient {
    private final RestClient client;

    OrdersClient(PlatformRestClientFactory factory) {
        this.client = factory.builder("orders").baseUrl("https://orders.internal").build();
    }

    Order get(String id) {
        try {
            return client.get().uri("/orders/{id}", id).retrieve().body(Order.class);
        } catch (RemoteCallException e) {
            throw new UpstreamOrdersFailure(e.status());
        }
    }
}
```

## Resilience

From the outside in: **deadline, retry, circuit breaker, bulkhead, HTTP**. Each attempt asks the breaker
and the bulkhead separately. All of it runs below the client's interceptors, so every attempt carries
the same token and `traceparent`, and one call is one `http.client.requests` observation.

- **Retry.** GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT and DELETE: on a connection failure, a timeout, or 429, 502, 503,
  504. Not on other 4xx, and not on 500, which is usually a bug that repeating only loads further.
  Default 3 attempts, waits jittered up to 200 ms, 400 ms, capped at 5 s. `Retry-After` replaces the wait;
  if it passes the deadline the call stops at once.
- **POST and PATCH are never retried**, with or without an `Idempotency-Key`, which passes through
  unchanged. Listing them in `retry.methods` fails startup.
- **PUT and DELETE are retried** because RFC 9110 calls them idempotent. If yours is not, remove them from
  `retry.methods`.
- **The JDK client re-sends a GET or HEAD once by itself** after a dropped connection, and this cannot be
  switched off per client. So the worst case is 2 × `max-attempts` requests. POST is not re-sent, and
  `jdk.httpclient.enableAllMethodRetry`, which would change that, stops the application from starting, as a system
  property or in the JDK's `conf/net.properties`. The check reads the file when the context starts; restart the JVM after changing it.
- **Only known idempotent methods follow redirects.** A POST, PATCH or custom method gets the 3xx back, since a 307 or
  308 would send it again. Under HTTP/2, the JDK can re-send a stream the server said it never processed.
- **Request bodies are held in memory** for the length of the call, so a streaming upload is buffered. Use something
  else for large uploads.
- **Deadline.** Always on. Covers all attempts and waits, from the moment a call reaches the client's transport: not
  the time your own interceptors or a slow upload callback take first. An attempt's timeout is the smaller of `read-timeout` and
  what remains. The read timeout covers the whole response, body included, so raise it for a large download.
- **Circuit breaker.** Per client name: opens at 50% failures over 10 calls, stays open 30 s, then allows 3
  trial calls. A failure is a connection failure, a timeout, or 500 and above. A 4xx is an answer. Open means
  nothing is sent and nothing is retried.
- **Bulkhead.** A semaphore per client name, default 25 calls and no waiting. The permit is held until the
  response closes. A thread-pool bulkhead is refused: it would pin blocking calls to platform threads.

A fallback is the caller's choice:

```java
try {
    return client.get().uri("/orders/{id}", id).retrieve().body(Order.class);
} catch (RemoteCallException e) {
    if (e.kind() == RemoteCallException.Kind.CIRCUIT_OPEN) {
        return cachedOrder(id);
    }
    throw e;
}
```

### What the caller of your service sees

An uncaught `RemoteCallException` becomes a ProblemDetail with code `DC-RCLIENT-0500` and a generic detail:

| Failure | Status | `retryable` |
|---|---|---|
| 429, 502, 503, 504, idempotent method | 503 | true |
| Any other 4xx, or 500 | 500 | false |
| Timeout or connection failure, idempotent method | 503 | true |
| Connection never made, any method | 503 | true |
| Deadline ran out, idempotent method | 504 | true |
| Breaker open, bulkhead full, any method: nothing was sent | 503 | true |
| POST or PATCH that may have arrived: the outcome is unknown | 500 | false |

### Metrics and health

- `platform.restclient.attempts{client,outcome}`: one per attempt. Outcomes: `success`, `status_4xx`,
  `status_5xx`, `timeout`, `connection`, `deadline`, `circuit_open`, `bulkhead_full`.
- `resilience4j.circuitbreaker.*` and `resilience4j.bulkhead.*`, tagged `name=rest-<client>`.
- The `restclient` health contributor is always `UP`, with each breaker's state in its details. It is in the
  `dependencies` group and never in readiness: a remote being down must not take every replica out.

Client names name breakers and tags, so take them from a fixed set. Query strings and URL credentials are left out of
the `uri` tag and the span's `http.url`.

A **success** body that cannot be parsed fails as Spring's `RestClientException`, with the parser's exception type and no text
from the body (HI-0099), so a secret in a broken response stays out of your logs. Converters you add after `builder()` returns
are not covered. A connection failure while reading a body is the `RemoteCallException` itself, and the table above applies.

## Properties

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `dc.platform.restclient.enabled` | `true` | Kill switch for the whole capability. |
| ~~`dc.platform.restclient.propagate-correlation`~~ | — | Removed (deprecated, level `error`): `traceparent` is always propagated. |
| `dc.platform.restclient.defaults.connect-timeout` | `2s` | Default connect timeout. |
| `dc.platform.restclient.defaults.read-timeout` | `10s` | Bound on one attempt's whole response, body included. |
| `dc.platform.restclient.defaults.deadline` | `30s` | Bound on one call, all attempts and waits included. |
| `….retry.enabled` | `true` | Retry idempotent methods. |
| `….retry.max-attempts` | `3` | Attempts, the first included. |
| `….retry.initial-backoff` | `200ms` | Upper bound of the first wait. |
| `….retry.multiplier` | `2.0` | Growth of the bound. |
| `….retry.max-backoff` | `5s` | Largest bound. `Retry-After` is limited by the deadline instead. |
| `….retry.methods` | `GET,HEAD,OPTIONS,PUT,DELETE` | A subset of these. |
| `….circuit-breaker.enabled` | `true` | Use the breaker. |
| `….circuit-breaker.failure-rate-threshold` | `50` | Percentage that opens it. |
| `….circuit-breaker.sliding-window-size` | `10` | Calls measured. |
| `….circuit-breaker.minimum-calls` | `10` | Calls needed before it can open. |
| `….circuit-breaker.open-duration` | `30s` | How long it stays open. |
| `….circuit-breaker.half-open-calls` | `3` | Trial calls after that. |
| `….bulkhead.enabled` | `true` | Use the bulkhead. |
| `….bulkhead.type` | `SEMAPHORE` | `THREAD_POOL` fails startup. |
| `….bulkhead.max-concurrent` | `25` | Calls at once. A full bulkhead refuses at once. |
| `dc.platform.restclient.clients.<name>.*` | (defaults) | Any of the above except `enabled` at the top, for one client. Unset values inherit. |

`…` is `dc.platform.restclient.defaults` or `dc.platform.restclient.clients.<name>`.

(Hand-written until the generated reference lands in phase 14.)

## Customize

```java
@Bean
@Order(10)
PlatformRestClientCustomizer apiKeyCustomizer() {
    return (name, builder) -> {
        if ("orders".equals(name)) {
            builder.defaultHeader("X-Api-Key", apiKey);
        }
    };
}
```

## Replace / Disable

- Define your own `PlatformRestClientFactory` bean to replace the default entirely.
- `dc.platform.restclient.enabled=false` switches the capability off wholesale.
- Calling `requestFactory(...)` on a builder, or in a customizer, removes retry, deadline, breaker and bulkhead
  from that client, along with the mapping of connection failures.

## Testing

Point a client at a `MockWebServer`/`WireMock`/JDK `HttpServer` instance via its base URL; no Docker
or network beyond your own test double is required. The service archetype's `restclient` feature
generates `client/GreetingClientTest`, which drives the real factory-built client against a loopback
stub (JSON both ways, empty bodies, 404/503 mapping, a bounded read timeout, a refused connection, and
correlation + token relay from a real authenticated inbound request).

## Local dev notes

No Docker, no network beyond the remote services you actually call.

<!-- source: modules/resilience.md -->

# Resilience

> **Coming in iteration 2.** This capability is parked: it is built and tested in the repository but not released in 1.0.0, not in the BOM and not offered by the archetype. Iteration 2 of the [Spring-native plan](../spring-native/plan.md) reworks it (Phase 9, as part of the REST client); this page describes the pre-rework design.

Fault-tolerance for calls to unreliable dependencies, built on [Resilience4j](https://resilience4j.readme.io/).
The platform contributes sensible default tuning and a small programmatic helper; the programming
model is Resilience4j's own annotations — the platform ships **no** wrapper annotations over them.

## What you get

- **Default instance tuning** — the `default` named configuration for each Resilience4j registry,
  contributed as lowest-precedence `resilience4j.*` environment defaults (your `application.yml`
  always wins):
  - retry: 3 attempts, exponential backoff (200ms × 2)
  - circuit breaker: opens at a 50% failure rate over a 10-call count window
  - time limiter: 5s, for `CompletionStage` and `Future` returns only; **it does nothing to a blocking call**
  - the default retry ignores `RemoteCallException` and Spring's `RestClientException` (see below)
- **`RetryableOperation`** — a programmatic retry helper (`<T> T call(String name, Supplier<T>)`) for
  call sites that cannot use the `@Retry` annotation (dynamic policy names, non-Spring call sites).
  The `name` resolves against the same retry registry the annotations use.
- **`ResilienceDefaults`** — the default values as constants, so application code and the platform
  share one source of truth.
- **Metrics** — Resilience4j's Micrometer binding is on by default, so retries, breaker state, and
  time-limiter events are instrumented when Micrometer/actuator are present.

**A call through `PlatformRestClientFactory` needs none of this.** That client already has its own
deadline, safe retries, breaker and bulkhead (see [REST Client](restclient.md)). Under the `default`
config, `@Retry` and `RetryableOperation` leave its failures alone: repeating one could send a POST twice,
and would multiply the retries of the rest. A retry instance of your own with `ignore-exceptions` changed loses
that protection. Use this capability for everything else: a file, a cache, a third-party SDK.

When several annotations are used together, Resilience4j's order, from the outside in, is
Retry, CircuitBreaker, RateLimiter, TimeLimiter, Bulkhead.

With `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true`, configuring `resilience4j.thread-pool-bulkhead` fails startup: use
`resilience4j.bulkhead`. An `@Bulkhead(type = THREADPOOL)` annotation is not detected, so don't use one.

## Starter coordinates

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform</groupId>
  <artifactId>platform-starter-resilience</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

## Usage

Declarative (preferred) — Resilience4j's own annotations, tuned by the platform defaults:

```java
@Retry(name = "inventory")
@CircuitBreaker(name = "inventory")
public InventoryLevel check(String sku) { ... }
```

Programmatic — when a policy name is dynamic or the call site is not a Spring bean:

```java
String stock = retryableOperation.call("stock-file", () -> readStockFile(path));
```

Override any default with Resilience4j's native keys:

```yaml
resilience4j:
  retry:
    instances:
      inventory:
        max-attempts: 5
```

## Properties

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `dc.platform.resilience.enabled` | `true` | Kill switch for the whole capability. |
| `resilience4j.retry.configs.default.*` | 3 attempts, exp backoff | Platform retry defaults (Resilience4j keys; overridable). |
| `resilience4j.circuitbreaker.configs.default.*` | 50% / 10-call window | Platform breaker defaults. |
| `resilience4j.timelimiter.configs.default.*` | 5s | Platform time-limiter default. |

The `resilience4j.*` keys and their metadata are documented by Resilience4j itself; the platform only
supplies the `default`-instance values at lowest precedence.

## Replace / Disable

- Define your own `RetryableOperation` bean to replace the platform helper (it backs off).
- Override any `resilience4j.*` key in `application.yml` — your value always wins over the defaults.
- `dc.platform.resilience.enabled=false` switches the capability off and skips the default
  contribution entirely.

## Local dev notes

No Docker required. Retry, circuit-breaker, and time-limiter behavior are proven with in-process
Resilience4j registries.


---

<!-- source: testing.md -->

# Testing platform services

The platform ships a test kit so a service tests the same way the platform is built: one starter,
composed slice annotations, ready fixtures, and Technology Compatibility Kits (TCKs) that certify
provider implementations. Everything here runs **docker-free** by default; real-infrastructure tests
are opt-in behind `@Tag("docker")`.

## One dependency

Add the test starter in **test** scope — it brings the platform test kit, `spring-boot-starter-test`
(JUnit 5, AssertJ, Mockito, spring-test), the recording messaging transport, and `json-path`:

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform</groupId>
  <artifactId>platform-starter-test</artifactId>
  <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
```

## Slice annotations

Compose a test context with one annotation (all activate the `test` profile and in-memory providers,
so no Docker/network/credentials are needed; logs keep the deployment JSON format — only the `local`
profile switches to console — so tests can assert structured log events):

| Annotation | Boots | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| `@PlatformTest` | the whole platform with test defaults | service/wiring tests |
| `@PlatformMessagingTest` | messaging autoconfig + a `@Primary` `TestEventTransport` | publish/handler assertions without a broker |
| `@PlatformDataTest` | Spring Boot's JPA slice on H2 + platform JPA conventions | repository/entity tests |
| `@PlatformWebTest` | mock web environment + `MockMvc` + the full error/validation/security stack | controller tests |

```java
@PlatformMessagingTest
class OrdersEventsTest {
    @Autowired TestEventTransport transport;
    @Autowired OrderService service;

    @Test void publishesOrderPlaced() {
        service.place("order-1");
        assertThatEvents(transport).sentTo("dc.orders").withType("OrderPlaced");
    }
}
```

> `@PlatformDataTest` needs the data capability on the test classpath (Hibernate); it is declared
> optional on `platform-test-api` so a non-JPA service is not forced to pull it in.

## Fixtures

- **`TestTokens`** — JWT identities for `MockMvc`, for a service that adds Spring Security's OAuth2
  resource server itself (1.0.0 ships no web security):

  ```java
  mvc.perform(get("/orders/42").with(TestTokens.user("alice").roles("VIEWER").jwt()))
     .andExpect(status().isOk());
  ```

  `TestTokens` bypasses the JWT decoder, so it cannot prove token *validation*. For that, use
  **`TestJwtIssuer`** — a loopback JWKS endpoint plus RS256 tokens (valid, expired, or signed by an
  untrusted key), no IdP or network:

  ```java
  static final TestJwtIssuer ISSUER = TestJwtIssuer.start();

  @DynamicPropertySource
  static void issuer(DynamicPropertyRegistry registry) {
      registry.add("spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.jwk-set-uri", ISSUER::jwkSetUri);
  }
  // real HTTP: "Authorization: Bearer " + ISSUER.token("alice")  → 200; ISSUER.expiredToken("alice") → 401
  ```

- **`assertThatProblem(...)`** — AssertJ assertions over RFC-9457 `ProblemDetail` bodies, including
  the platform `code`/`traceId` extensions:

  ```java
  assertThatProblem(response).hasStatus(404).hasCode("DC-ORD-0001");
  ```

- **`Containers` + `DockerAvailable`** — shared, lazily-started singleton Testcontainers for
  `@Tag("docker")` tests, guarded so they skip when no Docker is present:

  ```java
  @PlatformTest
  @Tag("docker")
  class OrdersRepositoryIT {
      @BeforeAll static void docker() { assumeTrue(DockerAvailable.check()); }

      @TestConfiguration
      static class Infra {
          @Bean @ServiceConnection PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres() { return Containers.postgres(); }
      }
  }
  ```

## TCKs — certifying a provider

Each multi-provider capability ships an abstract **TCK**: extend it, supply your provider, and
inherit the whole contract suite. A provider is *platform-certified* iff the TCK passes against it.

| Capability | TCK | Certified docker-free | Under `@Tag("docker")` |
|---|---|---|---|
| messaging | `EventTransportTck` | in-memory transport | RabbitMQ |

```java
class MyTransportTckTest extends EventTransportTck {
    @Override protected EventTransport transport() { return new MyTransport(...); }
}
```

Some invariants are **relaxable** for backends that genuinely cannot meet them, via a protected
`boolean` hook the subclass overrides (documented on each TCK). 

The TCK jars are published (Test Support category), so enterprise providers built on the platform SPIs
self-certify by depending on the TCK in test scope.

## Running

- Default (docker-free): `mvn -T1C verify` — the in-memory transport passes its TCK.
- Full matrix (Docker running): `mvn -Pdocker verify` — adds the `@Tag("docker")` certifications.

<!-- source: examples.md -->

# Examples

Four runnable services under [`examples/`](https://github.com) build inside the platform reactor and
consume the platform exactly as a real service does — through `platform-service-parent` and the
`platform-starter-*` dependencies. They are never published (`maven.deploy.skip`) and never part of
the [BOM](reference/bom.md); their `example-` artifactId prefix marks them as demonstrations to the
dependency-constitution enforcer.

Run any of them from its module directory with `mvn spring-boot:run`, or boot-and-probe the whole
stack with `tooling/scripts/golden-path.sh` (archetype) and `tooling/scripts/smoke-matrix.sh`
(golden-path across capability combinations).

## example-minimal — the floor

`platform-starter-core` + `-errors` + `-logging`, and nothing else. It exists to prove the smallest
thing the platform guarantees:

- every request carries a correlation ID and structured JSON logs, with no code in the service doing
  it;
- a thrown [`NotFoundException`](modules/errors.md) renders as an RFC-9457
  `application/problem+json` 404 with a stable [error code](reference/error-codes.md) — there is
  deliberately no `@RestControllerAdvice` anywhere in the service.

`GET /ping` returns `{"status":"ok"}`; `GET /widgets/{id}` always throws, so the problem-response
path is always exercised. See [`ProblemResponseTest`](modules/errors.md) for the assertion.

## example-golden-path — the canonical reference

The service to read first. A small **orders** domain (`POST /orders`, `GET /orders/{id}`) wired through
the 1.0.0 stack: REST + Spring validation + [observability](modules/observability.md)
+ [JPA/H2](modules/data.md) + [messaging](modules/messaging.md) (in-memory locally). It has no web
security: in 1.0.0 the API gateway authenticates callers. Every
cross-cutting concern comes from a `platform-starter-*`; `OrderService` is a tour of the APIs a service
actually calls (`OutboxPublisher`, `@Transactional`, `NotFoundException`),
and the class deliberately contains no error, security, or serialization code.

Run it with `mvn -pl examples/example-golden-path spring-boot:run`. Messaging is in-memory here;
`example-event-driven` shows a real broker over RabbitMQ.

Tests, all through the platform slices and Docker-free:

- `OrderFlowTest` (`@PlatformWebTest` + `@AutoConfigureTestTransport`) — `POST /orders`
  persists, publishes `OrderPlaced` (asserted on `TestEventTransport`), and is read back;
- `OrderProblemResponseTest` — unknown order → 404 problem with code, invalid body → 400 problem;
- `PlatformSurfaceTest` — `/actuator/platform` reports capabilities;
- `StartupBudgetTest` — cold-start wall-clock stays within the checked-in baseline + 15% (deliverable C).

## example-event-driven — producer/consumer over messaging

Two services — `example-event-driven-producer` and `example-event-driven-consumer` — that communicate
only through platform [messaging](modules/messaging.md). The producer publishes `ShipmentRequested`
via `EventPublisher`; the consumer receives it with `@EventHandler`. Each service owns its own copy of
the event record, as separate deployables do; the platform matches them by JSON shape and the
`eventType` header.

The **retry/DLQ** behaviour is the headline. `ShipmentHandler` throws for a shipment whose id is
`poison`; `ShipmentRetryDlqTest` delivers one and asserts the platform made three attempts and then
republished the message to the DLQ destination (`dc.shipments.dlq`) — all Docker-free over the
in-memory `TestEventTransport`. `ShipmentRoundTripTest` covers the happy path.

Both services run on **RabbitMQ**, the only transport (the tests need no broker). Start it, then the two services:

```
docker compose -f docker-compose.local.yml up -d rabbitmq
mvn -pl examples/example-event-driven/producer spring-boot:run
mvn -pl examples/example-event-driven/consumer spring-boot:run
```

# Configuration properties

> Generated by `PropertiesReferenceGenerator` from every module's `spring-configuration-metadata.json` at build time. Do not edit by hand.

Every platform property lives under the `dc.platform.<capability>` prefix, has a default in code, and is overridable in `application.yml`. Each capability's kill switch is `dc.platform.<capability>.enabled` (default `true`).

## dc.platform.core

| Key | Type | Default | Description | Deprecation |
|-----|------|---------|-------------|-------------|
| `dc.platform.core.banner-enabled` | Boolean | `true` | whether the startup capability banner is logged |  |
| `dc.platform.core.correlation.generate-if-missing` | Boolean |  | Removed: a request without a valid traceparent always starts a new trace, whose trace ID is the correlation id. | error (The tracing bridge always starts a new trace when traceparent is missing or invalid.) |
| `dc.platform.core.correlation.header-name` | String |  | Removed: the correlation id is the W3C trace ID and travels in the standard traceparent header, so there is no custom header to configure. | error (Correlation is the W3C trace ID (traceparent); custom correlation headers are no longer read or written.) |
| `dc.platform.core.enabled` | Boolean | `true` | master kill switch for the whole capability |  |

## dc.platform.data

| Key | Type | Default | Description | Deprecation |
|-----|------|---------|-------------|-------------|
| `dc.platform.data.jpa.enabled` | Boolean | `true` | master kill switch for the whole capability |  |
| `dc.platform.data.jpa.oracle.flyway-read-timeout` | Duration | `10m` | read timeout on Flyway's own connection (user or url), so a long migration statement (an index build) can finish while a silent database still fails startup |  |
| `dc.platform.data.jpa.oracle.read-timeout` | Duration | `60s` | read timeout on every connection of an Oracle pool: the longest the driver waits for an answer; above the 30 s transaction default, so a slow statement is cancelled by that first. Raise it for a service whose transactions are longer |  |
| `dc.platform.data.jpa.require-migrations` | Boolean | `true` | fail startup when JPA is configured but Flyway is absent; set to false to run JPA without managed migrations |  |

## dc.platform.errors

| Key | Type | Default | Description | Deprecation |
|-----|------|---------|-------------|-------------|
| `dc.platform.errors.enabled` | Boolean | `true` | master kill switch for the whole capability |  |
| `dc.platform.errors.include-rejected-values` | Boolean | `false` | echo each invalid value as rejectedValue (off by default: rejected values are raw user input and may be personal data; credential-shaped fields stay redacted even when on) |  |
| `dc.platform.errors.include-stacktrace` | Boolean | `false` | add a stacktrace extension to problem bodies (debugging aid; never enable in production) |  |
| `dc.platform.errors.map-validation` | Boolean | `true` | map Bean Validation failures to 400 problem responses with errors[] |  |
| `dc.platform.errors.type-base-uri` | String | `urn:dc:problem:` | base URI prepended to the error code to form the problem type |  |

## dc.platform.logging

| Key | Type | Default | Description | Deprecation |
|-----|------|---------|-------------|-------------|
| `dc.platform.logging.enabled` | Boolean | `true` | master kill switch for the whole capability |  |
| `dc.platform.logging.format` | ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform.logging.autoconfigure.LoggingProperties$Format | `json` | log output format; json in every deployed environment, console for humans (auto-selected when the local profile is active) |  |
| `dc.platform.logging.include-mdc` | Boolean | `true` | copy MDC entries (traceId, spanId, …) into JSON log fields |  |
| `dc.platform.logging.mdc.include` | List<String> |  | MDC keys written besides traceId and spanId; empty (the default) writes every MDC key, a non-empty list switches to strict mode and drops unlisted keys |  |
| `dc.platform.logging.redaction.enabled` | Boolean | `true` | mask values (on by default) |  |
| `dc.platform.logging.redaction.patterns` | List<String> |  | additional regular expressions whose matches are masked |  |
| `dc.platform.logging.service-name` | String |  | service name stamped on every JSON log line; defaults to name |  |

## dc.platform.messaging

| Key | Type | Default | Description | Deprecation |
|-----|------|---------|-------------|-------------|
| `dc.platform.messaging.correlation.propagate` | Boolean |  | Removed: messages carry the W3C traceparent, and a handler continues the producer's trace; there is no correlation header to switch off. | error (Correlation is the W3C trace ID, carried in traceparent on every message.) |
| `dc.platform.messaging.default-destination-prefix` | String | `dc.` | conventional prefix applications may use when naming destinations (not enforced; a naming convention only) |  |
| `dc.platform.messaging.dlq.suffix` | String | `.dlq` | appended to a destination name to form its DLQ destination, e.g. orders" |  |
| `dc.platform.messaging.enabled` | Boolean | `true` | master kill switch for the whole capability |  |
| `dc.platform.messaging.handler.retry.backoff` | Duration | `1s` | pause before the second attempt; doubles per attempt |  |
| `dc.platform.messaging.handler.retry.max-attempts` | Integer | `3` | total attempts before the message is dead-lettered |  |
| `dc.platform.messaging.handler.retry.max-backoff` | Duration | `30s` | the longest pause between attempts |  |
| `dc.platform.messaging.outbox.batch-size` | Integer | `50` | the most rows claimed in one transaction, and so the most duplicates a killed instance can cause |  |
| `dc.platform.messaging.outbox.enabled` | Boolean | `true` | false publishes after commit, no longer guaranteed, and logs a WARN saying so |  |
| `dc.platform.messaging.outbox.gauge-interval` | Duration | `5s` | how often the backlog metrics are refreshed |  |
| `dc.platform.messaging.outbox.initial-backoff` | Duration | `1s` | the first per-row retry delay; doubles per attempt |  |
| `dc.platform.messaging.outbox.max-backoff` | Duration | `5m` | the longest per-row retry delay and the longest pause after a failure |  |
| `dc.platform.messaging.outbox.max-rejections` | Integer | `10` | how many times the sink may reject a row before it is parked; outages do not count |  |
| `dc.platform.messaging.outbox.poll-interval` | Duration | `1s` | the pause when nothing is due |  |
| `dc.platform.messaging.outbox.pool-size` | Integer | `2` | the most database connections the drainer holds, on its own pool; at least 2 |  |
| `dc.platform.messaging.outbox.read-timeout` | Duration | `60s` | the Oracle driver's read timeout on the drainer's connections, unless the application pool sets one |  |
| `dc.platform.messaging.outbox.retention-interval` | Duration | `5m` | how often sent rows are deleted |  |
| `dc.platform.messaging.outbox.sent-retention` | Duration | `24h` | how long a sent row is kept before deletion |  |
| `dc.platform.messaging.outbox.statement-timeout` | Duration | `30s` | the timeout on each statement the drainer runs |  |
| `dc.platform.messaging.outbox.stop-timeout` | Duration | `30s` | how long a shutdown waits for the batch in flight |  |
| `dc.platform.messaging.rabbit.confirm-timeout` | Duration | `5s` | how long a send waits for the broker's publisher confirm before it fails |  |
| `dc.platform.messaging.rabbit.delivery-limit` | Integer | `20` | returns a quorum queue allows before dead-lettering: catches a message that keeps killing its consumer, which in-process retries cannot count. A message merely held by a stopping consumer counts too, so it is well above what rolling restarts reach |  |
| `dc.platform.messaging.rabbit.prefetch` | Integer | `10` | how many messages a consumer holds at once, and so how many a retrying handler can delay |  |
| `dc.platform.messaging.rabbit.quorum-queues` | Boolean | `true` | declare quorum queues, the main and the dead-letter one; false for classic queues |  |
| `dc.platform.messaging.rabbit.shutdown-timeout` | Duration | `30s` | how long a stopping consumer waits for the handler in flight |  |

## dc.platform.observability

# Error codes

> Generated from `platform-errors-autoconfigure/target/error-codes.csv` (emitted by `ErrorCodeRegistryTest`) at build time. Do not edit by hand.

Every platform error carries a stable `DC-<CAP>-<NNNN>` code. Codes are unique platform-wide (enforced by the phase-04 registry gate) and surface in RFC-9457 problem responses. See [errors](../modules/errors.md).

| Code | Capability | Declared by |
|------|------------|-------------|
| `DC-CORE-0400` | core | `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform.errors.autoconfigure.PlatformExceptionHandler` |
| `DC-CORE-0410` | core | `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform.errors.autoconfigure.PlatformExceptionHandler` |
| `DC-CORE-0499` | core | `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform.errors.autoconfigure.PlatformExceptionHandler` |
| `DC-CORE-0500` | core | `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform.errors.autoconfigure.PlatformExceptionHandler` |
| `DC-DATA-0409` | data | `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform.errors.autoconfigure.internal.DataAccessFailure$Codes` |
| `DC-DATA-0410` | data | `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform.errors.autoconfigure.internal.DataAccessFailure$Codes` |
| `DC-DATA-0503` | data | `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform.errors.autoconfigure.internal.DataAccessFailure$Codes` |
| `DC-TEST-0001` | test | `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform.errors.autoconfigure.internal.ProblemDetailFactoryTest` |

<!-- source: reference/bom.md -->

# Platform BOM

> Generated from `build/platform-bom/pom.xml` at build time. Do not edit by hand.

Import one BOM to align every platform artifact to a single release-train version (ADR-005). Then add only the starters you need — a capability you don't add costs you nothing.

```xml
<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform</groupId>
      <artifactId>platform-bom</artifactId>
      <version>${platform.version}</version>
      <type>pom</type>
      <scope>import</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>
```

## Managed artifacts

| Artifact | Version |
|----------|---------|
| `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform:platform-dependencies` | `${revision}` |
| `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform:platform-build-tools` | `${revision}` |
| `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform:platform-core-api` | `${revision}` |
| `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform:platform-core-autoconfigure` | `${revision}` |
| `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform:platform-starter-core` | `${revision}` |
| `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform:platform-errors-api` | `${revision}` |
| `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform:platform-errors-autoconfigure` | `${revision}` |
| `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform:platform-starter-errors` | `${revision}` |
| `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform:platform-logging-api` | `${revision}` |
| `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform:platform-logging-autoconfigure` | `${revision}` |
| `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform:platform-starter-logging` | `${revision}` |

| `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform:platform-starter-data-jpa` | `${revision}` |
| `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform:platform-starter-data-jpa-oracle` | `${revision}` |
| `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform:platform-test-api` | `${revision}` |
| `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform:platform-starter-test` | `${revision}` |
| `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform:platform-tck-messaging` | `${revision}` |
| `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform:platform-mcp-server` | `${revision}` |
| `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform:platform-skill` | `${revision}` |
| `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform:platform-migrations` | `${revision}` |

<!-- source: reference/compatibility.md -->

# Compatibility

The platform ships as a single release train (ADR-005): every `platform-*` artifact shares one
version, and SemVer applies to the train as a whole.

## Binary compatibility guarantee

> Within major version **N**, any application or extension compiled against platform **N.x** public
> API/SPI runs unmodified on every **N.y** (y ≥ x). Internals carry no guarantee. Majors may break
> with a published migration guide and automated OpenRewrite recipes.

| Surface | Package | Promise |
|---|---|---|
| Public API | `…​.<cap>`, `…​.annotation`, config keys | binary-compatible within a major; checked by japicmp against the last released minor |
| SPI | `…​.spi` | binary-compatible within a major; **new default methods allowed** in minors |
| Auto-configuration class names | `…​.autoconfigure` | semi-public (used in `exclude=`); renamed only at majors, old name kept as a deprecated forwarder for one minor |
| Internal | `…​.internal` | **no guarantee**; may change in patches; excluded from japicmp and javadoc |

## japicmp reports

Binary-compatibility is enforced by the japicmp gate over `-api`/`-spi` packages. The gate is armed
once the first release is tagged (`0.1.0`); before that it runs in report-only mode.

Per-release japicmp reports are published alongside the docs site under `apidocs/` and linked from
each [upgrade note](../upgrade/0.2.0.md) as trains are cut. No comparison baseline exists yet for the
current `0.2.0-SNAPSHOT` development train.

## Related

- [ADR-005 — release-train versioning](../decisions/adr-005.md)
- [Upgrade runbook](../runbooks/upgrade.md) · [Release runbook](../runbooks/release.md)


---

<!-- source: operations/adoption.md -->

# Platform adoption

How to see, per environment, which platform train each service runs and which capabilities it uses.
Everything here is derived from metrics the platform already emits — no separate reporting to wire.

## The signals

| Signal | Source | Emitted by |
|--------|--------|-----------|
| `platform.version` (common tag on every meter) | the platform jar manifest | observability common-tags (`CommonTagsAutoConfiguration`) |
| `platform.capability.active{capability=...}` gauge (0 or 1) | each capability's `CapabilityDescriptor` | observability `CapabilityMetricsAutoConfiguration` (phase-16 F.1) |
| deprecated-property warnings | Spring Boot's `spring.config` deprecation logs | log pipeline (count by service) |

`platform.capability.active` is `1` when a capability is active in a service and `0` when it is
present but inactive (for example, messaging on the classpath with no transport). Toggle it off with
`dc.platform.observability.capability-metrics.enabled=false`.

## What to track

- **Trains in production** — distinct `platform.version` values across `up` services, so you can see
  the spread and who is behind.
- **Capability adoption %** — `avg by (capability) (platform_capability_active)` across services.
- **Deprecated-property warnings** — count of Boot deprecation warnings per service, a leading
  indicator of upgrade friction.
- **Services on N‑2 or older** — anything more than two trains behind the current release, the
  support-window edge (see [upgrade](../upgrade/1.0.0-RC1.md)).

## Dashboard

`tooling/dashboards/platform-adoption.grafana.json` is an importable Grafana dashboard (Prometheus
data source) with panels for the four items above. Import it and point it at the environment's
Prometheus. The release pipeline links a per-train snapshot into the release notes once a Grafana
instance is available (phase-16 F.3).

<!-- source: runbooks/local-dev.md -->

# Runbook — Local Development

## Prerequisites
Java 25 (the reactor requires it; the enforcer's `RequireJavaVersion` fails otherwise), Maven 3.9+,
git. Docker Desktop OPTIONAL (only for `-Pdocker` and manual infra).

## Everyday commands
```bash
mvn -T1C verify                                   # full build+tests, no Docker needed
mvn -T1C -pl <path/to/module> -am verify          # one module + its dependencies
mvn -T1C install                                  # put platform into ~/.m2 for local apps
./tooling/scripts/golden-path.sh                  # end-to-end DX check (after phase 13)
```

## Docker-backed tests & manual infra
```bash
docker compose -f docker-compose.local.yml up -d  # rabbitmq, oracle (Oracle Free)
mvn -Pdocker verify                               # runs @Tag("docker") suites (Testcontainers manages
                                                  # its own containers; compose is for MANUAL app runs)
docker compose -f docker-compose.local.yml down -v
```
Connection details are in `docker-compose.local.yml`.

## Running an example against real infra
```bash
docker compose -f docker-compose.local.yml up -d rabbitmq
mvn -pl examples/example-event-driven/producer spring-boot:run   # and the consumer, in a second shell
```
The golden-path example runs on H2 and the in-memory transport; `example-event-driven` uses RabbitMQ.

## Debugging platform behavior in an app
1. `--debug` flag → ConditionEvaluationReport: why each platform auto-config did/didn't activate.
2. `GET /actuator/platform` → capability status + active providers.
3. `GET /actuator/env` → look for `platform-<cap>-defaults` property sources (platform-set defaults; anything above them overrides).
4. Startup log line `platform: …` lists capabilities.
5. Kill switch a capability: `dc.platform.<cap>.enabled=false`.

## Troubleshooting
- **Build fails in enforcer `PlatformLayerRule`** → the message names the violated edge and the fix; do not add exclusions.
- **japicmp failure** → you broke public API/SPI binary compat; either restore, or (major only) follow [release](release.md) deprecation path.
- **Docker tests fail with "Docker not available"** → expected without Docker; they must be `assume`-skipped — if they FAIL instead, the guard is missing (fix the test).
- **`${revision}` weirdness in IDE** → reimport Maven; flatten plugin handles publishing, IDE uses raw poms.

## Rendering these docs
The Markdown sources build and are gated (completeness + link check) by the default `mvn -T1C verify`.
The HTML site is an opt-in render (it shells out to MkDocs, which is not a Maven-Central tool):
```bash
pip install mkdocs-material                        # one-time: the render tool (not a Maven dep)
mvn -Pdocs-site -pl docs/platform-docs verify      # builds site/ via mkdocs
python -m http.server -d site 8000                 # browse at http://localhost:8000
```


---

<!-- source: runbooks/new-capability.md -->

# Runbook — Adding a New Capability

1. **Decide the shape.** One implementation plausible → api + autoconfigure + starter.
   ≥2 providers plausible → add spi + one LOCAL provider first (inmemory/fs/jdbc), then real providers.
   Never create an SPI with a single conceivable implementation.
2. **Scaffold:** `mvn ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform:platform-build-maven-plugin:new-module -Dcapability=<cap> -Dkind=api` (repeat per kind).
3. **Write the API** with full javadoc (coding-standards §2). Get it reviewed BEFORE autoconfigure —
   API is the irreversible part.
4. **Autoconfigure** from the autoconfigure pattern: properties record, kill switch, back-off,
   customizers, CapabilityDescriptor, imports file.
5. **Starter POM(s)**, one per provider.
6. **Tests:** ContextRunner matrix + behavior tests; provider TCK if multi-provider (copy an existing TCK's shape);
   docker-only tests tagged + assumption-guarded.
7. **Docs:** `docs/modules/<cap>.md` using the mandatory template sections. The
   [completeness gate](../reference/properties.md) fails the build if a starter has no capability page
   or a property is undocumented.
8. **Wire:** platform-bom, root modules, CHANGELOG.
9. **Verify:** module `-am verify`, root `verify`, golden-path script still green.
10. **Error codes:** claim a namespace (`DC-<CAP>-…`) in the registry (the uniqueness test will police
    it, and the code appears in the [error-codes reference](../reference/error-codes.md)).

See also: [extension model](../concepts/extension-model.md) · [conventions](../concepts/conventions.md).


---

<!-- source: runbooks/release.md -->

# Runbook — Cutting a Release Train

## Versioning recap
Single train version for all artifacts. SemVer: patch = fixes only; minor = additive (new modules,
new default methods on SPIs, new properties); major = breaking (removals, Boot major). See
[ADR-005](../decisions/adr-005.md) and [compatibility](../reference/compatibility.md).

## Local rehearsal (always do this first)
```bash
git switch main && git pull && git status   # clean tree recommended (rehearsal only warns if dirty)
./tooling/scripts/release.sh 1.0.0-RC1 --rehearse
```
Rehearsal runs, in order: verify at `-Drevision=<v>` → `golden-path.sh` → `smoke-matrix.sh` →
release notes (`target/release-notes-<v>.md`, from conventional commits since the last tag) →
aggregate japicmp compatibility report (`docs/reference/compatibility-<v>.md`) → deploy to a
file:// staging repo under `target/staging-repo` via `-Plocal-release`. It never tags or pushes.

## Real release
```bash
./tooling/scripts/release.sh 1.0.0-RC1     # runs the same gates, then tags v1.0.0-RC1 (no push)
git push origin v1.0.0-RC1                  # pushing the tag triggers release.yml: deploy + docs + notes
```
A real release refuses a dirty tree and a pre-existing tag. CI (`release.yml`) re-runs the gates with
deploy credentials, performs the real `mvn deploy`, and regenerates notes/compat via
`release.sh <v> --notes-only`.
Then: bump `<revision>` to next `-SNAPSHOT` on main; move CHANGELOG Unreleased → 0.2.0 section;
write `docs/upgrade/0.2.0.md` (highlights, deprecations, ACTION REQUIRED — may be "none").

## Patch train (hotfix)
Branch from tag `vX.Y.Z` → `release/X.Y` → fix + test → release.sh X.Y.(Z+1) from that branch.
Security fixes: target <48h; only the fix, nothing else rides along.

## Gate checklist (release.sh enforces; human confirms)
- [ ] root verify green, docker suite green on CI nightly
- [ ] japicmp: no binary breaks in -api/-spi (or major + migration guide + OpenRewrite recipe)
- [ ] golden-path + smoke-matrix green
- [ ] docs build with version banner; property/error-code references regenerated
- [ ] CHANGELOG + upgrade note written
- [ ] examples build against the new train in the N-1 nightly job (`release.yml` `compat-n-1`; a no-op
      until the first tag exists, then it builds the previous tag's examples against the current BOM)


---

<!-- source: runbooks/upgrade.md -->

# Runbook — Upgrading a Service to a New Train (for application teams)

1. Read `docs/upgrade/<version>.md` — do everything under **ACTION REQUIRED** first (for this train:
   [0.2.0](../upgrade/0.2.0.md)).
2. Bump one number: the `<version>` of `platform-service-parent` in your pom (or `platform.version`
   property if you consume the BOM directly).
3. Run the checker:
   ```bash
   mvn ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform:platform-build-maven-plugin:upgrade-check -Dplatform.target=<version>
   ```
   Fix every deprecation it reports (it names the replacement key/type). Warnings today are removals
   at the next major — do not defer.
4. `mvn verify`. Startup WARNs about deprecated properties count as failures for this checklist.
5. Smoke locally: app boots, `/actuator/platform` capabilities all ACTIVE as expected, key flows pass.
6. Majors only: apply the published OpenRewrite recipe first
   (`mvn org.openrewrite.maven:rewrite-maven-plugin:run -Drewrite.recipeArtifactCoordinates=ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform:platform-migrations:<v>`),
   then steps 1–5.
7. Stuck? Check `--debug` condition report + the capability page's "Replace/Disable" section before
   filing a platform issue; include your `/actuator/platform` output.

See also: [compatibility](../reference/compatibility.md) · [release runbook](release.md).
