  `KeyValidator` (path-traversal guard) and no provider interface. Chosen the simpler option per
  CLAUDE.md "when the spec is silent / two options": one fewer contract type to evolve, and provider
  selection is by classpath (fs default, S3 when present) exactly like locking/idempotency, not by a
  named-provider lookup.
- **D48 — filesystem sidecar uses Jackson.** The spec calls for a JSON metadata sidecar next to each
  object file. Rather than hand-roll a JSON writer (which would mis-escape arbitrary user-tag values —
  quotes, newlines, unicode), the fs provider depends on Boot-managed `jackson-databind` to serialise
  `ObjectMetadata`. Jackson is the fs provider's declared 3rd-party lib (impl-rule compliant); the
  version is inherited, not pinned.
- **D49 — storage checksum spools to a temp file.** The spec wants a SHA-256 computed on put and
  stored as a user tag, but the API is streaming-first (no `byte[]`, objects can exceed heap) and an
  `InputStream` can't be read twice. `ChecksumObjectStore` spools the content once through a
  `DigestInputStream` to a temp file, then hands the spool to the provider — bounded by disk, not
  memory. The alternative (buffer into heap) is the exact footgun the API forbids; the alternative
  (skip the tag, expose only the provider etag) fails the "stored as user tag" requirement. Trade-off:
  one extra disk write per put when checksums are on; toggle off via
  `dc.platform.storage.checksum.enabled=false`.
- **D50 — phase 10 ships storage + flags; secrets deferred.** The team manages secrets via Helm
  (injected as environment variables) and, locally, plain environment variables — which Spring Boot's
  relaxed binding already consumes natively, making the phase-10 secrets `env` provider redundant and
  the Vault provider unneeded today. Secrets is self-contained (nothing depends inbound on it; phases
  11–16 do not require it), so it was dropped from this phase and can be added later in its own PR with
  zero changes to storage/flags. Log redaction, the one real loss, is available via a user-registered
  `LogSanitizer` bean (the SPI ships in `platform-logging-api`). Consequently phase-10 delivers docs ×2
  (storage, flags), not ×3, and the `-Pdocker` vault suite is not present.
- **D51 — audit_jdbc stores the details map as a CLOB JSON document.** The `AuditEvent.details` map
  is schemaless by design (arbitrary structured context per action), so `JdbcAuditSink` serialises it
  to JSON with Jackson (the sink's declared 3rd-party lib alongside spring-jdbc) and stores it in a
  single `CLOB` column rather than modelling per-key columns. CLOB is H2-tested here; PostgreSQL
  deployments map CLOB→TEXT (Flyway runs the DDL against the target engine). The alternative
  (key/value child table) adds a join and write per detail entry for data that is only ever read back
  whole. Trade-off: details are not queryable by key in SQL; that is acceptable for an append-only
  trail whose primary consumers are the log pipeline and export.
- **D53 — the messaging audit sink is its own autoconfigure module, not an impl and not folded into
  the main audit autoconfigure.** The messaging sink must reference `EventPublisher` (messaging-api).
  An impl module may not depend on another capability's api (constitution: reach other capabilities
  from the autoconfigure layer), so the spec's `audit-messaging` cannot be an impl. Folding it into
  `platform-audit-autoconfigure` instead pushed that module to 7 platform dependencies (api, spi,
  core, log-sink, jdbc-sink, security-api, messaging-api) — over the autoconfigure fan-out ceiling of
  6. Resolution: `platform-audit-messaging-autoconfigure` is a dedicated autoconfigure module (cap
  `audit`) contributing the messaging `AuditSink`, guarded by `@ConditionalOnClass(EventPublisher)`.
  Ordering across modules (messaging > jdbc > log) uses name-based `@AutoConfigureAfter`, so no
  autoconfigure→autoconfigure dependency is introduced. It is not bundled in `platform-starter-audit`,
  keeping messaging-api off the classpath of audit consumers who do not use messaging.
- **D54 — rate-limit rejection is its own exception type, not a BusinessException.** The errors
  capability's `HttpStatusHint` is a closed 4xx enum with no 429 value, and adding one would change an
  errors contract. So `@RateLimited` rejection throws `RateLimitExceededException` (ratelimit-api,
  carrying the retry-after), and the ratelimit autoconfigure registers a Spring-MVC `@RestControllerAdvice`
  mapping it to a 429 `ProblemDetail` with `Retry-After`. The HTTP-filter path writes its own 429
  problem+json because a servlet filter runs before MVC exception handling. Both paths therefore emit
  RFC-9457 problem+json with a Retry-After header, without touching the errors capability.
- **D55 — the default content-type validator is a magic-byte table, not Tika.** The spec offered
  "Tika-core pin? prefer simple magic-bytes table for the v1 set". `MagicBytesContentTypeValidator`
  recognises PDF/PNG/JPEG/ZIP by signature and CSV/plain-text by a printable-byte scan (comma before
  the first newline ⇒ CSV). No `tika-core` dependency, no transitive footprint; a service needing
  broader detection supplies its own `ContentTypeValidator` bean. Trade-off: the v1 set is small and
  CSV/text detection is heuristic — acceptable for validating the platform forms' accepted uploads.
- **D56 — StreamingDownloads lives in files-autoconfigure, not files-api.** The spec lists it under
  api, but its signature returns `ResponseEntity<StreamingResponseBody>` over a storage `ObjectStore`
  — a Spring-web type and another capability's type, both forbidden in an api signature (api →
  core-api only; no third-party types in api signatures). It ships as a public helper in the files
  autoconfigure module (guarded by the storage capability on the classpath), reachable by consumers
  through the starter. `FileUploadPolicy` and `SafeFilename` remain in the dependency-poor api.

## Phase 12 — test kit & TCKs

- **D57 — `secrets` TCK omitted.** The phase-12 spec lists `platform-tck-secrets`, but the secrets
  capability (phase-10 §B) was never built — there is no `Secrets` SPI or provider to certify. The
  five TCKs with real providers ship (messaging, storage, locking, flags, ratelimit); the secrets TCK
  is deferred until the capability exists.
- **D58 — enforcer models the test-kit shapes.** `PlatformLayerRule` classified `platform-test-api`
  as API (suffix `-api`) and forbade the test starter from aggregating Test Support modules — neither
  shape existed when the phase-2 enforcer was written. Two minimal, tested changes: `*-test-api` is
  Test Support (checked before `-api`), and the `test`-capability starter may aggregate any non-starter
  module (still never another starter). The gate was re-verified to still fire on a seeded violation.
- **D59 — test-api package layout dodges the api-root rule.** All test-api types live one level below
  `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform.test` (`.junit`, `.container`, `.security`, `.assertj`) so the ArchUnit
  "api root packages carry contracts only" rule (which matches `platform.<cap>[.annotation]`) does not
  constrain this dependency-rich Test Support module.
- **D60 — capability kits are optional on test-api; the `Containers` class is coverage-excluded.**
  messaging/data test deps are `optional` so a service only pulls what its slices use (the starter
  re-declares the messaging bits it bundles). `Containers` starts real Docker containers, so it cannot
  execute docker-free and is excluded from the module coverage ratio (mirroring the parent excluding
  `*AutoConfiguration`); everything else is covered by self-tests.
- **D61 — docker-tagged provider certifications deferred.** The repository has no `@Tag("docker")`
  tests in any prior phase, and constructing real Kafka/Rabbit/Redis/S3/Vault wiring that cannot be
  run here would risk the docker-free reactor. This phase ships the abstract TCKs, the docker-free
  reference certifications (in-memory/fs/JDBC), and the `Containers`/`DockerAvailable` fixtures; the
  Kafka/Rabbit/Redis/S3 certifications are added when the `-Pdocker` lane is first exercised. TCK jars
  are published so this is additive.
- **D62 — JDBC lock TCK relaxes strict concurrent exclusion on H2.** The provider acquires with two
  statements (reclaim-then-insert) on separate connections; H2's in-memory engine does not reliably
  serialize that under high concurrency (empirically 1-3 winners), so a strict one-winner assertion is
  flaky. The concurrent stress still asserts safety (>=1 winner, no error), and deterministic
  sequential-exclusion + fencing prove mutual exclusion docker-free; strict concurrent exclusion is a
  relaxable invariant certified against PostgreSQL under `@Tag("docker")`.

## Phase 13 — developer experience

- **D63 — the archetype parents to the bare root aggregator, not platform-parent.** A `maven-archetype`
  generator is neither a library nor part of the dependency constitution, and its packaging needs a
  literal `maven-archetype-plugin` version. Parenting to `dc-platform` (like `build/*`) exempts it from
  the enforcer's no-literal-version rule and the coverage gate. `check-bom` also learns to skip
  `maven-archetype` packaging (nothing depends on a generator through the BOM).
- **D64 — `PlatformUsageRules` lives in `platform-test-api`, package `...test.arch`.** The spec's
  illustrative "testing.arch" is aligned to the module's existing `...test.*` layout. ArchUnit is a
  managed (no-version) compile dependency there; rules match banned third-party types by FQN so the kit
  adds no Kafka/Rabbit/MVC dependency.
- **D65 — archetype integration test behind `-Parchetype-it`; golden-path is the real gate.** The
  archetype IT forks `mvn verify` on generated projects that resolve platform artifacts from the local
  repo, which a plain reactor `verify` has not installed. Binding it to the default build would break
  the reactor (ground rule 1). golden-path.sh installs first, so it is the end-to-end acceptance.
- **D66 — golden-path pins `maven-archetype-plugin:3.1.2`; the archetype uses no post-generate groovy.**
  3.2.0+ made `archetype:generate` fork a `generate-sources` lifecycle (`<executePhase>`) that requires
  a project and so fails project-less on Maven 3.9.x; 3.1.2 generates cleanly. 3.1.2 predates
  `archetype-post-generate.groovy` support, so feature-sample pruning is done with Velocity `#if`
  (empty-but-compiling files when a feature is off), `AGENTS.md` ships as a verbatim copy of `CLAUDE.md`,
  and the docs carry the platform's default docs URL + a `DC-XX` namespace placeholder rather than
  per-generation token substitution.
- **D67 — `UpgradeCheckMojo` is coverage-excluded; its logic lives in tested helpers.** The mojo is
  Maven/Aether resolution glue (resolve the target BOM + jars); `BomVersionDiffer`, `PropertyKeyCollector`,
  `MetadataDeprecations`, and `UpgradeReport` are pure and unit-tested offline. Same rationale as the
  `Containers` exclusion in `platform-test-api`.

## Phase 14 — documentation as a product

- **D68 — `<proc>full</proc>` in `platform-parent`; config metadata is regenerated, not hand-written.**
  Every `*-autoconfigure` module already declared `spring-boot-configuration-processor`, but JDK 23+
  javac no longer runs classpath-discovered annotation processors by default, so no
  `spring-configuration-metadata.json` was emitted anywhere (IDE autocomplete broken; phase-14 property
  reference empty). Enabling `full` honors each module's existing optional dependency and re-enables all
  classpath processors, not just the config one. ~23 modules now emit metadata.
- **D69 — `platform-docs` parents the ROOT AGGREGATOR, not `platform-parent`.** A docs module has no
  shippable Java surface, so `platform-parent`'s capability gates (jacoco coverage, ArchConstitutionTest,
  japicmp) do not fit; it follows the `platform-build-tools` precedent (D4). All logic is test-scope; the
  produced jar is intentionally empty; it is still listed in `platform-bom` for `check-bom` parity.
- **D70 — docs generators run as JUnit tests reading the reactor tree; ordering is forced by explicit
  test-scope deps on all `*-autoconfigure` modules.** The spec's "test-scope main() run at build" reads
  sibling `target/` (config metadata; errors-autoconfigure's `error-codes.csv`). Under `mvn -T1C` a
  module with no reactor edges is scheduled early/in parallel, which would silently produce an incomplete
  reference — so `platform-docs` depends (test scope, ordering only) on every autoconfigure module to
  build last.
- **D71 — MkDocs render is opt-in (`-Pdocs-site`); strictness is enforced in-JVM.** CLAUDE.md rule #2
  forbids the default reactor needing tools beyond Maven Central, and `mkdocs` is a Python tool. The
  completeness gate and a pure-JVM broken-link gate run in the ordinary `verify`; `mkdocs build` (and
  `-Papidocs` aggregate javadoc) only produce the browsable HTML under `docs/site/`.
- **D72 — generated `error-codes.md` carries code + capability + declaring class only.** The phase-04
  registry CSV contract is `code,declaredBy`; there is no description column to render, so the generator
  presents exactly what the registry gate owns rather than inventing prose.
- **D73 — examples use error-code namespace `DC-XMPL-####` and package `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.example.*`.**
  Keeps example error codes valid under the `^DC-[A-Z]{2,8}-\d{4}$` contract yet outside the platform's
  `ae.gov.dubaicustoms.platform` package, so the phase-04 error-code registry gate (which scans the
  platform package) never sees them and the `example-` artifactId keeps them enforcer-exempt.
- **D74 — `example-golden-path` names its JPA table `orders` via `@Table`.** `order` is a reserved SQL
  word; the derived DDL fails on H2/PostgreSQL. Tests use `*Test` naming (surefire) because the platform
  wires no failsafe, so an `*IT` class would silently never run.
- **D75 — `example-extension-provider` encrypts with AES-CTR, not GCM.** CTR is length-preserving, so the
  ciphertext size equals the plaintext size and the storage TCK's `ObjectRef.size`/`contentLength`
  assertions stay true through the decorator; the per-object IV is stashed in a reserved user-tag. A
  production note points at GCM + platform-managed keys.
- **D76 — `example-event-driven` selects its transport by Maven profile (`local`=in-memory default,
  `rabbit`=RabbitMQ), each module owning its copy of the event record.** The platform's transport
  auto-configs are first-wins by declaration order, so merely adding rabbit alongside in-memory would not
  switch; an `activeByDefault` `local` profile that deactivates under `-Prabbit` guarantees exactly one
  transport starter. Kafka is deferred until the infrastructure supports it.
- **D77 — the smoke matrix toggles kill-switch properties over one packaged jar, not per-combo rebuilds,
  and only toggles capabilities that degrade to no-ops (cache, audit).** Recompiling per starter combo
  cannot fit a time budget and the assertion target (the `/actuator/platform` report) is identical;
  messaging, data-jpa, and resilience are pinned present because the reference service injects their
  beans and cannot boot without them.
- **D78 — `release.sh` rehearsal degrades japicmp to a first-baseline report and `-Plocal-release` is
  declared on the root aggregator and `platform-service-parent`.** No train has been deployed, so
  japicmp (`ignoreMissingOldVersion=true`) has no baseline to diff. The deployable parents/BOM parent to
  the root aggregator while `platform-service-parent` sits off `spring-boot-starter-parent`, so the
  staging-repo profile must live in both to reach every deployable artifact.
- **D79 — apiguardian `@API(status, since)` is added alongside the existing `@PlatformApi` marker, not
  as a replacement (phase-16 A.1).** `@PlatformApi` stays because the enforcer/japicmp gates target it
  for SemVer breakage control; apiguardian carries the finer-grained, machine-readable stability status
  (STABLE / EXPERIMENTAL / DEPRECATED / INTERNAL) that consumers, agents, and the platform-index read
  straight from the jar. The two are complementary. The `@API`-presence ArchUnit rule is scoped to the
  published **contract surface** — api-root packages, any `.spi` package, the `core.context`/`core.report`
  api sub-packages, and the test-api packages — rather than every public type in the reactor: provider
  impl, autoconfigure, and internal types are wiring, not consumer contracts, so forcing a status on them
  would be noise. API-root types default to `STABLE`, SPI types to `EXPERIMENTAL` (extension points more
  likely to evolve). A companion rule enforces that apiguardian `DEPRECATED` and `java.lang.@Deprecated`
  **co-occur**, so deprecation is a guarantee both the compiler and machine readers see, never docs-only.

## Post-1.0-RC1 — scope & hygiene (2026-07 platform review)

- **D80 — `tenancy` (P3) and `secrets` (phase-10) are out of scope for the 1.0 train; Kafka ships
  un-exercised.** The 2026-07 platform review (`docs/reviews/platform-review-2026-07.md`) recorded that
  `tenancy` was never implemented (acceptable — P3/optional) and `secrets` was deferred while the
  reactor still carries references *around* its absence (a deferred FailureAnalyzer, a deferred Vault
  enforcer ban, the `noSystemGetenv` usage rule pointing at a "platform secrets property source", and
  the phase-10 spec). Rather than leave these as silent gaps, they are declared explicitly: tenancy is
  a candidate for a later train. **Secrets scope is superseded by D81** (below): after clarifying the
  consuming architecture, the decision is to *reconcile the references*, not build a capability — the
  original "secrets-api + secrets-env + autoconfigure + starter" plan in this entry is withdrawn. Kafka
  messaging remains in the catalog but has no example/smoke path (transport infra uses RabbitMQ, D76);
  it should be marked `EXPERIMENTAL` via `@API` until an end-to-end path exists. This decision only
  records scope; no code changed with it. The same review actioned Track 1 (doc/toolchain truth-gaps):
  architecture-doc + runbook version headers corrected to Boot 4.1 / Java 25, README docs pointer fixed,
  `docs/decisions/README.md` added to explain the ADR-vs-log split, `.mvn/jvm.config` committed, and
  stray JVM crash logs removed.
- **D81 — no secrets capability is built; the dangling references are reconciled to Spring Cloud Vault
  (supersedes the secrets portion of D80).** Clarifying the consuming architecture settled it: services
  read secrets from HashiCorp Vault via **Spring Cloud Vault** (`spring-cloud-vault-config`) as ordinary
  `${...}` property placeholders, and rotate **static-KV values by rolling pod restart** (Level-1
  consumption, no in-process `@RefreshScope`). Property injection is therefore native Spring and rotation
  is a Kubernetes-rollout concern, so a `secrets-api/spi/impl/autoconfigure` capability would wrap what
  Spring and K8s already do — confirming D50. The action (Track 2, `specs/phase-17-secrets.md`) is to
  re-point the four references at that sanctioned pattern: reword the `noSystemGetenv` rule (+ its
  javadoc/test/fixture/docs) to name Spring config placeholders instead of a platform source; drop the
  deferred `secrets-unresolvable-ref` FailureAnalyzer; drop the deferred `spring-cloud-vault` ban
  (Spring Cloud Vault is the *allowed* mechanism, not a banned one); and confirm the `platform-tck-secrets`
  omission (D57) stands. A POM-only convention starter (`platform-starter-secrets-vault`) that only
  standardizes Vault wiring is noted for later, to be built **only if** per-service config drift becomes
  a measured cost — at which point the `spring-cloud-vault` *direct-dependency* ban would be reinstated
  to steer teams to the starter. This entry records the decision; the reconciliation edits are pending.

- **D82 — TCKs added for audit and idempotency; none for cache (it has no SPI).** The 2026-07 review
  (Track 2.3) called for TCKs on cache, audit, and idempotency. Audit (`AuditSink` SPI, multiple sinks:
  log/jdbc/messaging) and idempotency (`IdempotencyStore` contract, JDBC default + Redis) each have a
  genuine provider contract, so `platform-tck-audit` (`AuditSinkTck`) and `platform-tck-idempotency`
  (`IdempotencyStoreTck`) ship as abstract contract suites and certify the shipped docker-free impls on
  H2 (`JdbcAuditSink`; `JdbcIdempotencyStore`). Audit's sinks are public modules, so the audit TCK
  certifies `JdbcAuditSink` in its own test; idempotency's store is internal to its autoconfigure module,
  so that module's tests (test-scope dep on the TCK, no cycle) certify `JdbcIdempotencyStore` while the
  TCK module itself certifies a reference in-memory store. **Cache gets no TCK:** `platform-cache-api`
  exposes only `CacheKeyConvention` + `CacheNames` and delegates caching to Spring's
  `CacheManager`/`Cache` — there is no platform cache SPI with multiple providers to certify, so a
  provider-TCK has no subject (certifying Spring's own `Cache` is not the platform's job); the key
  convention is a pure function already unit-tested. New `@since 1.0.0` types are `...tck.*` (Test
  Support), outside the apiguardian `@API`-required contract surface (D79), matching the existing TCKs.
- **D83 — archetype `features` is validated in the `pom.xml` template, not by `<validationRegex>`.**
  Batch-mode `archetype:generate` (3.1.2 and 3.4.0, verified) ignores `validationRegex`, and
  `archetype-post-generate.groovy` is not an option (3.4.0's Groovy cannot parse Java 25 class files).
  The first-processed template derives `",<features>,"`, strips each known token, and on anything left
  calls `String.matches` with an unclosed `[`; Velocity surfaces the exception text (which carries the
  actionable message) as the generation error. Every template matches tokens exactly (`",data,"`), so
  `database` can never enable `data`. A rejected generation leaves only a 0-byte `pom.xml`. This also
  corrects D66's rationale (re-tested on Maven 3.9.9 / JDK 25): 3.1.2 does run post-generate Groovy,
  and 3.4.0 generates project-less without error — the "requires a project" failure reproduces when
  PowerShell splits unquoted `-Dkey=a.b` arguments. 3.1.2 stays the documented, gate-tested version.
- **D84 — the archetype's `platformVersion` default is its own version, via filtering one file.**
  ADR-005 puts every platform artifact on one train, so the archetype version IS the platform version.
  Only `META-INF/maven/archetype-metadata.xml` is Maven-filtered; `archetype-resources` must stay
  unfiltered because its `${artifactId}`/`${version}` belong to Velocity at generation time.
- **D85 — generated `application.yml`: offline placeholders on `on-profile: "!prod"`; `prod` refuses
  embedded databases.** The JWKS placeholder, the open capability report, and the sample downstream URL
  apply to every profile except `prod`, so a production start without real coordinates hits the
  platform's existing failure analyzers (`JwtDecoder` / DataSource / unresolvable placeholder) instead of
  running on placeholders. `spring.datasource.embedded-database-connection=none` under `prod` stops Boot
  from silently falling back to the bundled H2. Chosen over required `${ENV}` placeholders: it reuses
  Boot's and the platform's own messages and keeps `application.yml` free of invented variable names.
- **D86 — `restclient` feature sample has no business endpoint.** Like the messaging and data samples,
  `GreetingClient` is a component only; its generated test drives it for real (loopback stub, and a
  test-only controller for the inbound → outbound correlation/token-relay chain). The packaged-jar gate
  therefore proves the client's registration and configuration, and the generated tests prove its
  calls.
- **D87 — `TestJwtIssuer` in the test kit, JDK-only.** Real bearer-token validation needs a JWKS the
  resource server can fetch. A reusable `platform-test-api` fixture (JDK `HttpServer` + JDK RSA
  signing, no third-party types in its API) serves generated services and the golden-path gate (which
  compiles its helper against the installed jar) instead of copying ~150 lines into every service.
- **D88 — startup budget measured in an isolated CI step.** `StartupBudgetTest` is a wall-clock
  guard. In the `-T1C` reactor it overlapped other modules' test contexts (docs snippet compilation,
  the event-driven examples) and measured 19-25 s against the 15 s baseline, although the same commit
  boots in the same time as `main` when measured alone. CI now skips it in the parallel `verify`
  (`-Dplatform.startup-budget.skip=true`) and runs it serially in its own step. Raising the baseline
  was rejected: it would hide the regressions the guard exists to catch.
- **D89 — correlation is the W3C trace ID (hardening HD5).** The platform-minted `X-Correlation-Id`
  is removed everywhere (core filter, REST client, tracing baggage, MDC key, ProblemDetail property).
  `CorrelationId`/`RequestContext` keep their API and carry the trace ID; inbound `traceparent`
  handling is left to Boot's observation filter and the OpenTelemetry W3C propagator. The platform
  filter moves to `HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + 10` (after the observation filter, before security).
  Without a tracer the platform establishes no correlation context rather than inventing an id.
- **D90 — no exception message in any 5xx body.** Including `PlatformException`s with status >= 500 and
  Spring MVC's own 5xx bodies; 4xx business messages stay (application-authored). Simpler and safer
  than classifying messages as safe.
- **D91 — `rejectedValue` off by default.** Field-name redaction cannot recognise personal data
  (national ID, email, phone); omitting the value by default is the allow-list default, opt-in via
  `dc.platform.errors.include-rejected-values`.
- **D92 — error-code uniqueness read from sources.** The classpath registry only sees the errors
  module's dependencies; a source scan over every platform module's `src/main/java` covers modules no
  single test classpath contains. Examples and the archetype are excluded (separate services).
- **D93 — overrides by type and by name; descriptors by name only.** Platform advice beans back off
  for a consumer bean of their type under any name, or any bean of their documented name.
  `CapabilityDescriptor` is one shared type with one bean per capability, so each descriptor backs off
  by name only.
- **D94 — the platform owns the servlet error page.** A `PlatformErrorController` replaces Boot's
  `BasicErrorController` (ordered before `ErrorMvcAutoConfiguration`), and the security chain permits
  the ERROR dispatch, so every error path — MVC, security, filters, the container — renders one
  problem contract. Spring Security's own guidance for error pages; the original request was already
  authorized or rejected on its REQUEST dispatch.
- **D95 — trace rejection judged by the propagator's outcome.** The core filter does not re-implement
  W3C validation: a present `traceparent` counts as rejected exactly when the current trace is not the
  one it names, and the marker carries the header length only.
- **D96 — shared-type infrastructure beans override by name.** *Superseded by D98.* The banner
  `ApplicationRunner` and the correlation filter's `FilterRegistrationBean` backed off by name only:
  consumers routinely define other beans of those Spring types, and type-based back-off would silently
  drop the platform's.
- **D97 — capability descriptors override by name, like Boot's health indicators (hardening A3).**
  `CapabilityDescriptor` is collected one-bean-per-capability, so type-based back-off would let any
  consumer descriptor remove every platform one. Spring Boot 4.1 makes the same choice for its collected
  health indicators (`@ConditionalOnMissingBean(name = "diskSpaceHealthIndicator")`, likewise
  `livenessStateHealthIndicator`, `readinessStateHealthIndicator`, `sslHealthIndicator`) while its
  single beans (`SslInfo`) back off by type. The capability kill switch `dc.platform.<cap>.enabled`
  removes the descriptor with the capability. Each remaining capability's descriptor gets the same
  guard and a real-override test in its own hardening phase.
- **D98 — single infrastructure beans override by type (supersedes D96).** The correlation filter is
  registered the way Boot registers its own `ServerHttpObservationFilter`: one
  `FilterRegistrationBean<CorrelationIdFilter>` with the filter created inline, guarded by
  `@ConditionalOnMissingFilterBean(CorrelationIdFilter.class)`, so a consumer `CorrelationIdFilter` bean
  or `FilterRegistrationBean<CorrelationIdFilter>` under any name replaces it, and unrelated filter
  registrations do not. `CorrelationIdFilter` is `Ordered` at `FILTER_ORDER`, so a consumer filter bean
  that Boot registers keeps the platform's position and dispatch types. The banner is a public
  `PlatformBannerRunner` class backing off by type; unrelated `ApplicationRunner` beans no longer matter.
- **D99 — neutral problem `type` default `urn:dc:problem:` (hardening HI-0010).** Supersedes the
  `type-base-uri="https://errors.dc.com/"` default in `specs/phase-04-errors-logging-validation.md`: that
  host is not owned by the platform. RFC 9457 allows a non-dereferenceable `type`; `dc` is not an
  IANA-registered URN namespace, so the value is an opaque identifier that services replace with an
  `https://` documentation base once one exists. 401/403 bodies read the same key and default.
- **D100 — no `replacement` for the removed correlation properties (hardening A1).** The
  `dc.platform.core.correlation.*` and `dc.platform.restclient.propagate-correlation` keys are
  deprecated at level `error` with a reason only: the correlation ID is now the W3C trace ID and has no
  successor property, so naming one would mislead.
- **D101 — the platform's own MDC emission is an allow-list; consumer MDC passes through (hardening
  phase 2).** Platform code writes only `traceId` and `spanId` (source-scan test). Consumer MDC keys keep
  reaching JSON logs, masked like every other value; dropping them by default would silently break
  services. Strict mode is opt-in: `dc.platform.logging.mdc.include` (non-empty: only `traceId`,
  `spanId` and the listed keys).
- **D102 — default log redaction set.** JWTs, `Bearer`/`Basic` credentials, values after credential keys
  (`password`, `secret`, `token`, `authorization`, `cookie`, `api-key`, …), whole values of
  credential-named MDC entries and structured arguments, Emirates ID, Luhn-valid 13–19 digit card
  numbers starting 2–6 (the issuer digit keeps epoch millis out), e-mail addresses and phone numbers
  (international with `+`/`00`, UAE mobiles in local form; owner request 2026-10-26) become `****`. Extendable with
  `dc.platform.logging.redaction.patterns`; `LogSanitizer` beans run first, the platform patterns last.
  Implemented as a logstash `ValueMasker`, so it covers message, MDC, arguments and stack traces alike.
- **D108 — no startup banner in JSON mode (hardening phase 2, Gate F trial).** The ASCII banner is
  written to stdout outside logging, so a log shipper parsing stdout line by line saw non-JSON lines.
  The logging EPP defaults `spring.main.banner-mode=off` whenever the JSON format is resolved
  (lowest precedence; `console` or `log` set by the service wins). Console format keeps Boot's banner.
- **D109 — `raw(...)` JSON is masked; unparseable raw text becomes a string (hardening phase 2, Gate D).**
  Logstash's masking generator forwards `writeRawValue` unread, so `raw("payload", "{\"password\":…}")`
  reached the log in clear. The platform reads the raw text as exactly one JSON value (member order,
  duplicates and exact numbers kept, escapes decoded) and writes it back through the masks. Text that
  is not one JSON value is written as a JSON **string**, escapes decoded, under the pattern masks:
  written raw it would make the whole line invalid JSON, and undecoded escapes (`password`)
  would hide credential names from the masks. Simpler than accepting the bypass as a residual, and
  fail-closed.
- **D110 — bounded data-access waits (hardening phase 3, Gate B).** Measured against Oracle before
  choosing: a statement cancel (JDBC query timeout, the JPA hint, a Spring transaction timeout) stops
  SQL work about a second after its limit, but not a PL/SQL or lock wait or a dead network. Defaults
  (lowest precedence): Hikari `connection-timeout` 5 s (was 30 s; a request behind an exhausted pool
  fails fast, 503); `spring.transaction.default-timeout` 30 s (bounds every transaction, repository
  methods included; note: it also applies to every transaction manager Boot creates, so Phase 4's
  outbox drainer inherits it unless it sets its own); on a `jdbc:oracle:` pool the driver's
  `oracle.jdbc.ReadTimeout` 60 s (above the transaction timeout, so slow SQL hits that first) and
  `oracle.net.CONNECT_TIMEOUT` 10 s, added by a BeanPostProcessor keyed on the pool's own URL (an
  environment check missed URLs from later property sources); leak detection 20 s under `local` only
  (never with `prod`). Hikari's keepalive and max lifetime stay its defaults. Round 1 (Gate C) added:
  a 30 s default query timeout (`jakarta.persistence.query.timeout`, `spring.jdbc.template.query-timeout`),
  because a declared repository query or a non-transactional service runs outside any transaction (measured:
  unbounded before); inside a transaction Spring sets the remaining time per query, which wins. And the
  Oracle driver bounds on Flyway's own `SimpleDriverDataSource` (`spring.flyway.user`/`url`), applied on
  the `Flyway` bean; residual: a `{vendor}` location connects before that (system properties cover it).
  Round 2 (Gate D): the remaining transaction time wins only for queries Spring creates as a
  `jakarta.persistence.Query` (repositories, the injected `EntityManager`, the unwrapped `Session`'s
  `createQuery`/`createNativeQuery`); Hibernate's `SelectionQuery` and raw-delegate queries take the query
  default (measured both ways). Decision: keep the default and document `.setTimeout(…)` on those paths
  rather than reaching into Spring's transaction or Hibernate's session internals — the statement stays
  bounded, and the alternative only approximates the remaining time. A pool started by the application
  (`new HikariDataSource(config)`, sealed) is now left alone instead of failing startup; a `Flyway` bean the
  application builds from a URL gets no driver bounds (Flyway's own data source; system properties cover it).
  Gate F (HI-0070, owner decision HD14): the read timeout bounds each wait for the database's answer, so a
  migration statement over 60 s (observed: a `CREATE TABLE` on a slow disk) failed startup, and a transaction given
  a longer `@Transactional(timeout)` was still cut at 60 s. Both are now properties:
  `dc.platform.data.jpa.oracle.read-timeout` (pool, 60 s) and `dc.platform.data.jpa.oracle.flyway-read-timeout`
  (Flyway's own connection, 10 min: an index build can finish, a silent database still fails startup). A
  `data-source-properties` entry or a JVM system property still wins. Migrations through the pool (no separate
  Flyway user) get the pool's value.
- **D111 — data-access failures are problems, classified by cause chain (hardening phase 3, Gate B).**
  Observed on Oracle: Spring translates only behind a repository proxy or at commit; `EntityManager`
  use lets raw Hibernate/JPA types through, and a batched insert reports a `BatchUpdateException`
  whose SQLState is the only sign of a constraint violation. The errors capability's catch-all
  therefore classifies the whole cause chain by class name (no compile dependency) and SQLState
  (`23` → 409 `DC-DATA-0409`, `40`/locking → 409 `DC-DATA-0410`, `08`/timeouts/no connection → 503
  `DC-DATA-0503`, retryable), with a fixed detail; a SQL bug stays 500. Simpler than a separate advice
  behind `@ConditionalOnClass`, which would miss the raw types and need ordering.
  Round 1 (Gate C) added `org.hibernate.PropertyValueException` (Hibernate's null check, before any SQL)
  as 409, and `org.hibernate.TransactionException` as 503 only with Hibernate's exact message
  `Transaction timeout expired` (a deadline passed before a flush or commit; pinned by an Oracle test).
  Gate F (consumer run, HI-0068): when the driver read timeout closes a connection mid-transaction, Spring rethrows
  the failed rollback in place of the 08006 cause, and Hikari's closed-connection `SQLException` has no SQLState.
  Hibernate's `Unable to rollback against JDBC Connection` over that closed-connection exception is a 503 (nothing
  was committed); over any other cause the cause classifies as usual. Codex verification added a veto: below
  Hibernate's `Unable to commit against JDBC Connection` nothing is classified, because a failed commit's outcome
  is unknown and a retry could apply the change twice (before, an 08006 cause made it a retryable 503). A second
  verification found Spring's translator drops that Hibernate exception (a recoverable SQLException cause becomes
  `RecoverableDataAccessException`), so a lost connection is also vetoed when it was raised inside Spring's
  `AbstractPlatformTransactionManager.processCommit` (by stack frame); a commit-time-flush conflict stays a 409 and
  Hibernate's deadline expiry stays a 503.
  HI-0069: Hibernate logs each failed statement's error code and driver message at WARN before the handler's WARN
  (three lines per violation, against scope R4 "logged once"). A default of `error` for that logger was tried and
  reverted on Codex verification: it also silences failures that application code catches, and batch or async
  paths without a handler. Decision: keep Hibernate's lines; the platform logs the exception once (scope
  amendment A2); `data.md` names the logger for services that want only the platform's line.
- **D112 — Flyway posture pinned; out-of-order refused outside `local` (hardening phase 3, Gate B).**
  `clean-disabled`, `validate-on-migrate`, `out-of-order=false`, `validate-migration-naming` are
  contributed explicitly so a Flyway upgrade cannot loosen them. The out-of-order guard is a
  bean post-processor on the `Flyway` bean: it checks the finished configuration (after every property and
  customizer, whatever its order) before Boot's migration initializer runs, with a `FailureAnalyzer`.
  Round 1 (Gate C) replaced a lowest-precedence customizer, which an equally ordered customizer could follow.
- **D113 — per-database starters; archetype `database` property (hardening phase 3, HD12).** One
  POM-only starter per certified database carries the JDBC driver and Flyway's database module, so the
  pair never travels apart (HI-0041). Only `platform-starter-data-jpa-oracle` exists (owner: other
  databases later). The archetype takes `-Ddatabase=h2|oracle` (default `h2`, unchanged output apart
  from a corrected comment); `oracle` requires the `data` feature and is validated like `features`.
- **D114 — `Instant` on Oracle is `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` (hardening phase 3, Gate B).** Hibernate
  maps `Instant` to its UTC timestamp type and reads an offset date-time; a plain `TIMESTAMP` column
  fails on read with ORA-18716. The platform keeps Hibernate's standard mapping rather than overriding
  the `Instant` JDBC type for every service and database; Oracle migrations declare `Instant` columns
  `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` (documented, tested across JVM and session zones).
- **D115 — the outbox is a JDBC module inside the messaging capability (hardening phase 4, HD11).** Owner's choice over
  the Spring Modulith event publication registry: every plan requirement (claiming, separate connection budget, parked
  state, trace columns) is explicit and testable, and a service adds no external framework. It belongs to messaging
  because the drainer sends through `EventTransport`, a messaging SPI, which another capability's autoconfigure may not
  use (rule 5). A separate `OutboxPublisher` makes guaranteed publishes visible in review. Its auto-configuration is its
  own module: the enforcer's fan-out ceiling refused it in `platform-messaging-autoconfigure`, and a service without the
  outbox then carries none of it.
- **D116 — lock while sending, not claim with a lease (hardening phase 4).** One transaction per batch: claim with
  `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, send, record, commit. The database releases a dead pod's locks, so no lease or recovery job
  exists, and a kill repeats at most one batch. The cost is a drainer connection and row locks held across sends, which
  the drainer's own pool isolates from requests. The batch limit stops the cursor fetch, because Oracle locks as it
  fetches; `ROWNUM` or `FETCH FIRST` would limit before skipping locked rows. Only a rejection by the sink counts toward
  parking, so a long outage parks nothing.
- **D117 — the drainer's pool is not a bean (hardening phase 4).** A `DataSource` or `PlatformTransactionManager` bean
  would make Boot back off from the service's pool or JPA transaction manager, and `@Transactional` would stop covering
  JPA writes. The pool is held by `OutboxConnections`, copied from a Hikari application pool so it inherits the Phase 3
  Oracle bounds; the drainer manages its own transactions and statement timeouts, so it does not inherit the 30 s
  transaction default (D110).
- **D118 — the outbox table is a copied migration (hardening phase 4).** A versioned migration in a platform jar collides
  with the service's sequence and can trip the out-of-order guard (D112); runtime creation fails for a runtime user
  without DDL rights. The DDL ships as a resource the service copies, and a startup check names it when the table is
  missing. An archetype feature was dropped: the archetype can only render an unwanted file empty, and an empty V2 would
  collide with the service's next migration (scope amendment A2).
- **D120 — One retry layer (hardening phase 5).** The registrar retries; a transport that dead-letters natively says so through
  `EventTransport.deadLettersNatively()`. Two layers multiplied attempts (3 configured, 9 measured). No delayed-retry queues: they
  need a plugin or more topology, and prefetch bounds what a backoff delays.
- **D121 — Quorum queues by default, with `x-delivery-limit` (hardening phase 5).** The limit is only for a message that keeps killing
  its consumer, which in-process retries cannot count.
- **D122 — Topology on every connection (hardening phase 5).** A service starts without the broker, since the outbox absorbs an
  outage, and a broker that lost its definitions gets them back.
- **D123 — A newer `eventVersion` goes to the DLQ (hardening phase 5).** Delivering risks misreading it; dropping loses it. A replay
  delivers it after upgrading. Unknown fields stay tolerated, so additive changes need no new version.
- **D124 — Replay through a dynamic shovel (hardening phase 5).** The broker moves the messages with confirms; a custom consumer
  could lose one mid-copy.
- **D119 — Rabbit publisher confirms and the event id brought forward from Phase 5 (hardening phase 4).** A row marked sent
  on an unconfirmed send could be lost, so "no loss" would be false; a row needs an id before it can be deduplicated. The
  rest of Rabbit (topology, consumers, DLQ, `traceparent` on `DefaultEventPublisher`) stays in Phase 5.
- **D102 addendum — compound credential names (hardening phase 2, Gate F trial).** A field or text key
  ending in `password`, `passwd`, `secret`, `token`, `apikey`, `authorization` or `cookie` (ignoring
  case, `-`, `_`) is a credential too: `sessionToken`, `x-auth-token`, `db_password`. The consumer run
  showed an MDC key `session-token` written in clear; over-masking a `…Token` field is the safer error.
  In text, `sessionCookie=…` masks its value like any credential key; only the exact `Cookie:` /
  `Set-Cookie:` header masks to the end of the line. The message view traverses structured values to
  64 levels and masks anything deeper or cyclic (fail closed): deep enough that ordinary payloads stay
  readable, bounded so a hostile value cannot exhaust the stack (verification pass 2).
- **D107 — console log format stays Boot's (hardening phase 2, A1, owner accepted 2026-10-26).** The
  `console` format (the `local` profile) is human-only: it is not masked and a CR/LF in a message can
  split a line. Overriding Boot's console pattern would fork its styling; JSON, used in every deployed
  environment, is masked and injection-safe.
- **D103 — sampling posture.** Head sampling stays Boot's (`management.tracing.sampling.probability`,
  default `0.1`). Keeping every errored request's trace is delivered by collector tail sampling
  (documented snippet); the platform position is OPEN as a deployment responsibility, as plan §9 Phase 2
  allows. Trace IDs in logs and problem bodies are independent of sampling.
- **D104 — readiness is pod-local (implements D6).** `readiness` = `readinessState`, `liveness` =
  `livenessState`; `db`, `rabbit`, `redis` move to a `dependencies` group for dashboards.
- **D105 — minimal actuator exposure.** Chassis default `health,info,prometheus`; `metrics` and
  `platform` are opt-ins. The archetype opts in `platform` because the generated docs, the golden path
  and the smoke matrix read it; access stays governed by security. Prometheus scraping is authenticated
  until the security phase decides between token, management port and permit rule.
- **D106 — uri tag cardinality is Boot's.** Boot 4.1 caps `uri` values for server and client HTTP
  meters (`management.metrics.web.{server,client}.max-uri-tags`, 100, deny + log once). The platform adds
  no `uri` filter of its own and keeps a test that fails if the cap is lifted.
- **D125 — Phase 5 residuals accepted (hardening phase 5, owner 2026-11-02).** HI-0087 and HI-0093 are accepted. HI-0088, a main queue
  deleted during a replay losing what the shovel moves afterwards, is accepted for now and goes back to the owner at the end of all
  phases, before the Phase 8 release decision: keep accepting it, or replace the shovel.
- **D126 — REST resilience in a request factory (hardening phase 6).** Below the interceptors, not an interceptor or aspect: a retried
  interceptor chain can skip later interceptors, such as the token relay, and the factory sees only real sends. One observation per call.
- **D127 — Resilience4j for the breaker and bulkhead, a short loop for retry (hardening phase 6).** Retry must weigh `Retry-After`, the
  deadline and the method together. Replacing the request factory removes all of it, documented. No `max-wait` on the bulkhead: a wait
  could pass the deadline, and a refusal is more useful than a queue. Only known idempotent methods follow redirects.
- **D128 — What is retried (hardening phase 6).** 429, 502, 503, 504, a timeout or a connection failure, on GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE
  (RFC 9110). Never POST or PATCH (HD2). Not 500: usually a bug, and repeating adds load.
- **D129 — `PlatformException.problemStatus()` (hardening phase 6).** A remote failure maps to 503, 504 or 500 through a hint on the core
  type, so `errors` stays independent of `restclient`. `BusinessException` keeps its own status hint.
- **D130 — An unknown outcome is never `retryable` (hardening phase 6).** A POST that may have arrived is 500, `retryable=false`, as a lost
  commit is under HI-0071's rule. A connection never made, or a local refusal, is 503 for any method.
- **D131 — Phase 6 residuals decided (hardening phase 6, owner 2026-11-02).** HI-0094, HI-0095, HI-0096, HI-0097 and HI-0098 are
  accepted, including HI-0096, which Codex rated High: the JDK caches the value privately, and the gap needs a JDK file edited on a live JVM.
  HI-0099 is **not** accepted and moves into Phase 7: the log encoder masks recognisable credentials in exception text, but a bare
  token has nothing to match, so the quoted text is removed at its source. `bodySnippet()` is to be treated as untrusted; the module
  docs' example no longer passes it on.
- **D132 — Phase 7 residuals accepted (hardening phase 7, owner 2026-11-03).** HI-0100 (a numeric `sub` or an overflowing `nbf`
  in a token the trusted provider signed), HI-0101 (the `@RequiresPermission` advisor fails startup rather than back off to a bean
  of its name, against plan §7.1, since that back-off switched enforcement off in round 1), HI-0102 (a UTF-16 body after an earlier
  filter took a UTF-16 writer) and HI-0103 (test gaps, no defect shown) are accepted, all Low, as Codex agreed in passes 2 and 3.
- **D133 — Spring Boot 4.1.2 and two security overrides (hardening phase 8, owner 2026-11-04).** Phase 8's scan (HI-0105) found 7
  Critical and 15 High known vulnerabilities in what a service ships, all in versions Boot 4.1.0 manages, among them an RCE in
  Spring WebMVC 7.0.8. Boot moves to 4.1.2 (Spring Framework 7.0.10, Tomcat 11.0.27, Netty 4.2.19, Jackson 2.21.7 and 3.1.7).
  `amqp-client` is pinned to 5.37.0 and OpenTelemetry to 1.67.0, which Boot 4.1.2 still manages at vulnerable versions. D17's
  Prometheus override is removed: Boot 4.1.2 manages 1.7.0. Phase 8 reruns on the new versions.
- **D134 — Phase 8 decisions before the release decision (hardening phase 8, owner 2026-11-04).** Step 7 (OpenShift, D7) is
  `BLOCKED`: the chart tool's location, invocation and a cluster were not supplied; it becomes a first-adopter condition, like
  RAC (HD4). HI-0088 stays accepted (D125 review). HI-0106 (CVEs in build and tooling modules and the uncertified Kafka path),
  HI-0107 (service jars not reproducible; two property references in `platform-dependencies`) and HI-0108 (no SBOM or
  provenance in the release pipeline) are accepted as release conditions; HI-0108 is to be done before the first real release.
- **D135 — Spring-native realignment, plan v2 (owner 2026-11-19).** On `develop` the platform is cut to seven
  capabilities in two iterations (1.0.0: logging, observability, data, RabbitMQ messaging and outbox; 1.1.0: REST API with
  basic auth and OpenAPI, REST client with basic auth and OAuth client credentials). Services use Spring types only; each
  capability is one autoconfigure module plus a POM-only starter (ND15). Decisions ND1 to ND15:
  [`docs/spring-native/decisions.md`](../spring-native/decisions.md).
- **D136 — Two recorded exceptions in the realignment plan (Phase 0 Codex review, 2026-11-19).** `OracleConnectionDefaults`
  stays a `BeanPostProcessor` (it only adds Oracle driver timeouts where none is set: HI-0061, HI-0063, HI-0070). In the
  closed hardening record, links to files the scope cut deletes are rewritten to tag `pre-spring-native`; nothing else in
  that record changes. Review: [`docs/spring-native/phase-00-baseline/review-round-1.md`](../spring-native/phase-00-baseline/review-round-1.md).
- **D137 — Phase 1 scope-cut choices (Spring-native Phase 1, 2026-11-19).** (1) The archetype keeps the in-memory
  messaging starter as its `messaging` default until Phase 6 moves messaging to Spring AMQP; switching to RabbitMQ first
  would make every generated test need a broker. (2) Parked modules set `maven.deploy.skip=true` and `check-bom` treats
  that as "not published": no BOM entry needed, and a BOM entry for one fails. (3) `platform-service-parent` drops its
  Resilience4j and springdoc bans while those starters are parked, rather than pointing services at a starter that is not
  released. (4) Without web security the generated `/actuator/platform` is exposed outside `prod` only, as before.


---

<!-- source: decisions/adr-001.md -->

# ADR-001 — Parent + BOM split

**Status:** Accepted

**Decision:** separate `platform-parent` (platform's own build), `platform-service-parent`
(applications), `platform-bom` (platform artifacts), `platform-dependencies` (third-party pins).

**Why:** applications must inherit conventions without inheriting the platform's internal build
machinery; BOM-only consumption must remain possible for Gradle teams and for teams with their own
parent.

**Consequence:** four small POMs to maintain; total decoupling of consumption styles.

See also: [dependency constitution](../concepts/constitution.md) · [conventions](../concepts/conventions.md).


---

<!-- source: decisions/adr-002.md -->

# ADR-002 — Starter philosophy

**Status:** Accepted

**Decision:** starters contain zero code; one starter per capability-provider pair; `starter-core`
is the only implicit starter.

**Why:** code in starters becomes un-excludable; per-provider starters keep classpaths minimal and
choices explicit.

**Consequence:** more starter POMs; trivially cheap.

See also: [extension model](../concepts/extension-model.md) · [platform BOM](../reference/bom.md).


---

<!-- source: decisions/adr-003.md -->

# ADR-003 — API vs SPI

**Status:** Accepted

**Decision:** separate artifacts and packages for consumer API and extender SPI; SPI exists only
when ≥ 2 providers are plausible.

**Why:** different audiences evolve at different speeds and need different compatibility promises;
merging them forces the slowest evolution speed on everything.

**Consequence:** more modules; crisp compatibility contracts; extenders never see internals.

See also: [extension model](../concepts/extension-model.md) · [conventions](../concepts/conventions.md).


---

<!-- source: decisions/adr-004.md -->

# ADR-004 — Auto-configuration as the only wiring mechanism

**Status:** Accepted

**Decision:** all platform behavior activates via `@AutoConfiguration` + conditions; no
`@ComponentScan` into platform packages, no `spring.factories` legacy, no programmatic registrars
beyond what conditions require.

**Why:** deterministic, debuggable (`--debug` report), AOT-analyzable, overridable by construction.

**Consequence:** condition-matrix tests are mandatory (§10).

See also: [conventions](../concepts/conventions.md) · [extension model](../concepts/extension-model.md).


---

<!-- source: decisions/adr-005.md -->

# ADR-005 — Release-train versioning

**Status:** Accepted

**Decision:** single version across all platform artifacts; SemVer on the train; no per-module
versions.

**Why:** eliminates the compatibility matrix; one tested set; one upgrade lever.

**Consequence:** a one-line fix ships a whole patch train — accepted; cheap with automated releases.

See also: [compatibility](../reference/compatibility.md) · [platform BOM](../reference/bom.md) · [upgrade runbook](../runbooks/upgrade.md).


---

<!-- source: decisions/adr-006.md -->

# ADR-006 — Module boundaries by capability, layered inside

**Status:** Accepted

**Decision:** vertical capability slices, each internally split api/spi/impl/autoconfigure/starter;
every module in exactly one category (§2.2).

**Why:** ownership, blast-radius control, and classpath minimalism follow capability lines, not
technical layers.

**Consequence:** many small modules; mitigated by scaffolding plugin and build caching.

See also: [architecture](../concepts/architecture.md) · [dependency constitution](../concepts/constitution.md).


---

<!-- source: decisions/adr-007.md -->

# ADR-007 — Dependency constitution enforced as code

**Status:** Accepted

**Decision:** the rules in §4 are executable (enforcer + ArchUnit + japicmp) and merge-blocking.

**Why:** prose architecture decays; failing builds don't.

**Consequence:** occasional friction on legitimate exceptions → ADR-gated rule changes.

See also: [dependency constitution](../concepts/constitution.md).


---

<!-- source: decisions/adr-008.md -->

# ADR-008 — Extension via Spring back-off + SPI, never modification

**Status:** Accepted

**Decision:** platform defaults always `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`; providers plug in by contributing
beans implementing SPIs; TCKs certify providers.

**Why:** open-closed at the ecosystem level; enterprises extend without forking; upgrades don't merge
conflicts.

**Consequence:** discipline required to never expose concrete classes as contracts.

See also: [extension model](../concepts/extension-model.md) · [testing](../testing.md).


---

<!-- source: decisions/adr-009.md -->

# ADR-009 — Why not a God Framework

**Status:** Accepted

**Decision:** no `platform-all`, no mega-core, `core-api` capped in size.

**Why:** transitive bloat, universal blast radius, CVE surface, native-image hostility, and the
coupling ratchet: every convenience added to a god module is permanent.

**Consequence:** teams add 3–8 starters instead of 1 artifact — the archetype writes those lines for
them.

See also: [architecture](../concepts/architecture.md) · [quickstart](../quickstart.md).


---

<!-- source: decisions/adr-010.md -->

# ADR-010 — Why Convention over Configuration

**Status:** Accepted

**Decision:** every capability works with zero configuration using documented conventions;
configuration exists to *deviate*.

**Why:** cognitive load is the platform's primary cost; conventions turn N team-decisions into 1
platform-decision made once by experts; consistency across hundreds of services is itself a feature
(operability, staffing mobility).

**Consequence:** conventions are API — changing a default is a breaking change and versioned as such.

See also: [conventions](../concepts/conventions.md) · [configuration properties](../reference/properties.md).


---

<!-- source: decisions/adr-011.md -->

# ADR-011 — Spring types in service code

**Status:** Accepted (2026-11-19, owner decisions ND3 and ND15). Refines [ADR-009](adr-009.md) and
[ADR-003](adr-003.md).

**Decision:** a service written on the platform imports Spring types, not platform types. The platform is
auto-configuration: it supplies property defaults, customizers and beans of Spring types, and steps back
when the service defines its own. Each capability is one Auto Configuration module and one POM-only
Starter. An API or SPI module exists only where no Spring type fits, and only with a recorded decision.

**Why:** a platform API is a second framework to learn, document and keep compatible, on top of Spring.
Spring Boot 4 already has a type for almost every extension point the platform wrapped (`RestClient.Builder`,
`RabbitTemplate`, `ProblemDetail`, `ApplicationEventPublisher`, ...). With one provider per capability,
an SPI has nothing to choose between.

**Consequence:** the platform's API modules are removed capability by capability
([Spring-native plan](../spring-native/plan.md)), and every guarantee they carried moves into
auto-configuration with a test. A guarantee that needs a platform type keeps one, named in an ND decision.

See also: [Spring-native decisions](../spring-native/decisions.md).


---

<!-- source: upgrade/1.0.0-RC1.md -->

# Upgrade notes — 1.0.0-RC1

> Train `1.0.0-RC1` (development continues on `1.0.0-SNAPSHOT`). This is the **M3 milestone** and the
> release candidate for `1.0.0`: the full capability catalog, the documentation site, four runnable
> examples, and a local-first release pipeline are all in place. Soak this RC, then cut `1.0.0`.

## ACTION REQUIRED

None. `1.0.0-RC1` is additive over `0.2.0`.

## Highlights

- **Four reference examples** ([examples](../examples.md)): `example-minimal` (the platform floor),
  `example-golden-path` (the canonical service — REST + validation + security + OpenAPI +
  observability + JPA + messaging + cache + resilience + audit over an `orders` domain),
  `example-extension-provider` (a custom `ObjectStore` certified by the storage TCK, proving the
  [extension model](../concepts/extension-model.md)), and `example-event-driven` (producer/consumer
  with `@EventHandler` retry/DLQ).
- **Smoke matrix.** `tooling/scripts/smoke-matrix.sh` boots the golden-path service across curated
  capability toggles and asserts `/actuator/platform` against a checked-in expectation table.
- **Startup-budget guard.** The golden-path example fails its build if cold-start wall-clock regresses
  more than 15% past a comment-governed baseline.
- **Release automation.** `tooling/scripts/release.sh <version> [--rehearse|--notes-only]` runs the
  gates, generates release notes from conventional commits and an aggregate japicmp compatibility
  report, and either stages to a `file://` repo (rehearsal, `-Plocal-release`) or tags the train;
  `release.yml` performs the real deploy on tag push. See the [release runbook](../runbooks/release.md).

## Messaging note

Kafka remains deferred until the infrastructure supports it. The real-broker example and profile
target **RabbitMQ**; the messaging API is transport-agnostic, so adopting Kafka later is a starter
swap, not a code change.

## Deprecations

None in this train.

## How to upgrade

Follow the [upgrade runbook](../runbooks/upgrade.md): bump the one version, run the upgrade checker,
`mvn verify`, and smoke-test locally.


---

<!-- source: upgrade/0.2.0.md -->

# Upgrade notes — 0.2.0

> Train `0.2.0` (development: `0.2.0-SNAPSHOT`). This is the **M2 milestone**: the golden path is
> complete — a service generated from the archetype builds, boots, and is probed end to end.

## ACTION REQUIRED

None. `0.2.0` is additive over `0.1.0`.

## Highlights

- **Golden-path complete (M2).** REST + errors + logs + metrics + tracing + security + messaging +
  JPA + tests + docs, generated by the [service archetype](../quickstart.md) in under 10 minutes.
- **Config metadata everywhere.** Every `@ConfigurationProperties` now emits
  `spring-configuration-metadata.json`, so IDEs autocomplete every `dc.platform.*` key and the
  [properties reference](../reference/properties.md) is generated from code.
- **Documentation as a product.** Generated [properties](../reference/properties.md),
  [error-code](../reference/error-codes.md), and [BOM](../reference/bom.md) references; the ten
  [ADRs](../decisions/adr-001.md); the four [runbooks](../runbooks/local-dev.md); and a completeness
  gate that fails the build if a property is undocumented or a starter has no capability page.

## Deprecations

None in this train.

## How to upgrade

Follow the [upgrade runbook](../runbooks/upgrade.md): bump the one version, run the upgrade checker,
`mvn verify`, and smoke-test locally.
